News.title: Two dead after military helicopter crashes in Texas as smash sparks wildfire & officials launch probe
News.content:
TWO pilots have been killed in a military helicopter crash after the chopper slammed into a field and burst into flames.

The deadly crash sparked a huge wildfire in Texas as dry grass quickly caught light, with firefighters battling the blaze for hours.



AH-64 Apache attack helicopter was based at the nearby US Army base of Fort Hood, the military said.

It crashed near the village of Salado, around 60miles north of Austin.





Emergency responders arrived to a huge blaze engulfing the chopper.

Officers had rushed to the scene at around 1.33pm after receiving reports about the wreckage.

Two minutes later, both pilots onboard were declared dead.

Bell County Sheriff’s Office spokesman Cliff Coleman said when they arrived the huge fire was already “getting out of control very quickly”.



He confirmed the chopper did not hit any structures or people as it fell out of the sky.

Coleman told reporters: “It crashed into a field, you could tell it was a violent crash.”

Dramatic photos showed the wreckage smoking as debris burnt in the dry grass.



A huge wildfire was sparked by the horror crash as the grass ignited, forcing locals to evacuate their homes.

The blaze tore through around 100 acres of land and took several hours to get under control.

Several local roads were closed as the inferno raged.

Acting commanding general at Fort Hood Brig. Gen. Ethan Diven told local news: “Our immediate priority is securing the site and supporting the initial response efforts.

“Our thoughts are with the crew and their families as we await further information.”



Texas Governor Greg Abbott wrote on X: “Today, an Apache helicopter crashed in Bell County during Fort Hood operations, killing two members of our military.

“Join Cecilia and me in prayer for their families and the entire Fort Hood community. Texas is forever indebted to those who serve our state and nation,” the governor said in the post.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

The identities of the pilots have not yet been released.

Officials launched an investigation into the accident.

News.title: Luxury villa used in James Bond film where spy says iconic catchphrase has ‘elegant’ apartment go up for sale
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

FOR YOUR KEYS ONLY

FOR YOUR KEYS ONLY Luxury villa used in James Bond film where spy says iconic catchphrase has ‘elegant’ apartment go up for sale

AN apartment in the luxurious Italian villa featured in Casino Royale has gone on the market.

The property – where James Bond delivers his iconic catchphrase – sits on the shores of glamorous Lake Como in northern Italy.



In the final scene of the first Bond film starring Daniel Craig, a black Jaguar pulls up the driveway of Villa La Gaeta.

Bond’s nemesis, Mr White, steps out of the car – only for a gunshot to ring out, sending the villain crashing to the ground.



Bond then appears in a full suit, gun in hand, and delivers the iconic line: “The name’s Bond, James Bond.”

Since the film’s release, the villa has become a magnet for Bond fans from around the world.



Until now, those wanting to experience the property could rent it for around €520 a night.

But an apartment inside the iconic villa is now being offered for sale by luxury property firm Sotheby’s International Realty.



The apartment features five rooms on the ground floor, with two bedrooms, a study and two bathrooms spread across two levels.

It also comes with two basement storage rooms and parking spaces.

“This property promises truly elegant living on Lake Como,” the estate agent told BILD.

Built in 1921 to designs by brothers Gino and Adolfo Coppedè, the property has a monthly maintenance fee of €400.

“As the owners, you don’t have to worry about anything on the property; a caretaker looks after the garden and the boat dock,” the listing says.



The Bond connection isn’t the only luxury on offer.

The south-facing terrace promises a “beautiful lake view” in the evening sun, according to the real estate agent.

The new owner will also have direct access to Lake Como, including a private beach.

There are boat berths in the villa’s private marina, a jetty and a swimming pool.

To sweeten the deal further, the complex is surrounded by sprawling parkland filled with “exotic and rare plants”.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

According to Sotheby’s, the apartment was renovated in 2023.

Anyone hoping to make this slice of Bond history their own will need to find €1.45 million.

News.title: ‘Afghan migrants pinned woman down’ and ‘raped her at knifepoint in sex attack’ at London park
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

PARK HORROR ‘Afghan migrants pinned woman down’ and ‘raped her at knifepoint in sex attack’ at London park

A WOMAN broke down in tears after allegedly being raped at knifepoint by two “Afghan males” in a London park, a court heard.

The victim was spending time with a male friend in Barking Park in East London on August 16, 2025.

The woman and her friend were then approached by Noorullah Ahmdzai, 26, and a co-defendant teenage boy, whose identity cannot be reported for legal reasons, the court heard.

Snaresbrook Crown Court heard that the pair pinned the woman to the ground before threatening her and her friend with a knife.





Giving evidence, the woman described one of her alleged attackers as having “a beard, not like a big one, a small one”.

She told the court: “He was talking in an accent, like people from Afghanistan talk. He pulled [my trousers] down.

“He was trying to kiss me.”

The woman then alleged that both men then proceeded to rape her.



Proceedings were briefly adjourned after she broke down during cross-examination by Ahmdzai’s barrister, Emily Culverhouse.

Ms Culverhouse put to the witness: “There was an agreement that you would have sex with both men for £70?”

“No, that is not true,” the woman replied, telling the court she had been forcibly restrained.

She added: “One of them was pushing me against the ground so that I can’t move, and the other person was on me.



“One of them was grabbing my legs.

“I don’t remember who tried to kiss me but one of them tried to kiss me.”

When the barrister alleged, “You complained because you wanted £500,” the woman answered, “No.”

Ms Culverhouse further pressed: “You said that you would call the police and make things bad for them?”

Ahmdzai, of Barking, east London, and his teenage co-defendant both deny rape, threatening another with a blade or point, and false imprisonment.



The teenager additionally denies assault by penetration.

The trial continues.

News.title: Moment Russian air defences desperately try to shoot down Ukraine attack as drones and missiles blitz Putin’s warships
News.content:
THIS is the shocking moment Russian air defences scramble to repel a Ukrainian blitz targeting the key Black Sea port of Novorossiysk.

Dramatic footage shows the night sky erupting as missiles streak upwards from Russian air-defence systems.



In separate footage, concerned witnesses gather around as smoke billows from the smouldering wreckage.

A third clip shows a water cannon battling to extinguish flames, while a line of cars backs up in the foreground.



The major attack on Novorossiysk destroyed warships and forced two major grain terminals to suspend operations.

Regional Governor Veniamin Kondratyev said at least two people were killed, including an eight-year-old girl.

Ukraine‘s SBU security service described the assault as being of “strategic significance”, saying the naval base was struck by a barrage of drones and missiles.

Volodymyr Zelenskyy said two frigates, a large landing ship, a corvette and other vessels were hit.



The strikes have also raised fears of disruption to global food supplies, with Russia among the world’s largest wheat exporters.

Russia’s Agriculture Ministry said it was working to establish alternative routes for exports.

One of the country’s main grain lobby groups warned last month that further attacks could shut down Black Sea grain exports entirely, potentially sending prices soaring.

Novorossiysk Mayor Andrei Kravchenko said the port suspended its water supply and declared a state of emergency following the strikes.

He said four businesses, more than two dozen residential buildings and several educational facilities were damaged.



The attack comes after heavy strikes on Ukrainian grain shipments in the Black Sea.

According to Ukraine’s Agriculture Ministry, shipments fell by 76 per cent in the first two weeks of August compared with the same period last year.

On Wednesday, Ukraine and Moldova also agreed a plan to route Ukrainian grain shipments through Moldova by rail.



Separately, more than three dozen drones were shot down over Sevastopol in Crimea on Wednesday.

As the bitter conflict enters its fifth year, Moscow has intensified strikes on Ukrainian logistics and warehouse facilities in response to attacks by Kyiv.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Zelensky said on Tuesday that Ukraine had handed US negotiators proposals for a plan to end the conflict.

Kyiv has repeatedly called for a ceasefire, while Moscow maintains that any settlement must involve Ukraine relinquishing territory.

News.title: Chancellor John Healey warned by voters to keep fuel duty freeze in place as pump prices soar
News.content:
VOTERS have warned Chancellor John Healey to keep the fuel duty freeze in place as prices soar.

Sixty-three per cent of Brits demand the rate be kept down as motorists grapple with high pump prices amid the Middle East conflict.



Pressure will mount on the Treasury in the run up to the Budget to maintain the freeze following The Sun’s 15-year campaign to help motorists.

Mr Healey also faces calls to extend the temporary 5p duty that is due to expire at the end of December.



Government documents say they will confirm the final rates at the Budget at the end of October.

A breakdown of the figures show 31 per cent strongly support a fuel duty freeze at its current rate with 32 per cent saying they somwhat support keeping the rate as it is.

Separately, 55 per cent say fuel duty should be reduced with 24 per cent say it should stay as it is.

Ex-Chancellor Rachel Reeves abandoned plans to hike fuel duty by 5p back in May in the aftermath of the Iran war.

Petrol hit 161.66p over the weekend as diesel has rocketed by 17p in a month now standing at 182p per litre.

A litre of petrol cost just 132.83p on the day the conflict broke out, while diesel cost 142.38p a litre.



Simon Williams, from the RAC, said: “The price of petrol appears to have finally reached an Iran War peak, having risen 11p over 33 consecutive days.

“While prices should fall a little in the coming days, this may be short-lived as the cost of a barrel of oil has climbed almost $10 in the last week towards $90.

“The current situation shows just how volatile fuel prices are and how drivers in the UK are at the mercy of global events.”

News.title: Cops turning on Burnham will be a big blow to the PM… He needs to be on THEIR side, not that of smirking killers
News.content:
WHEN Andy Burnham announced last year that Chief Constable Sir Stephen Watson was to remain at the head of Greater Manchester Police for a ­further two years, he did so with considerable pride.

Watson, he said, had delivered a ­“colossal turnaround” in the UK’s second- largest police force, making “significant strides” to ensure the city’s streets ­were safer, adding: “We are backing him to ­finish the job.”



There is no question that Watson is a real coppers’ copper who oversaw important changes in Manchester.

And that is why his signature on a letter from 50 police chiefs calling for the Prime Minister to block the release of two of PC Andrew Harper’s killers will have been a significant, and very painful, blow.



But this loss of confidence from Britain’s top cops has not happened overnight.

First there was the reaction of Thames Valley Police Chief Constable Jason Hogg, who said in August he was “beyond ­disappointed” that smirking killers Albert Bowers and Jessie Cole would be eligible for early release.

On Monday, he was joined by Thames Valley Police and Crime Commissioner, Matthew Barber, and Chair of the Thames Valley Police Federation, Aileen O’Connor, who wrote to Burnham urging him to keep the pair behind bars.

Their words show these police leaders understand the psychological impact of this debate on frontline officers.

They will have had conversations with them, which I can imagine — and I’m sure your readers can too — beginning with the words: “Boss, they don’t have our backs.”

Policing is on its knees, and those at the top understand that our officers need to feel the Government has their backs when they run towards danger — as PC Harper did.



The senior policing community do not always acquit themselves well when ­dealing with the state.

However, I believe their open letter today is driven by a genuine sense of ­outrage that politicians could be so callous as to forget the impact of the chaotic early release scheme on their officers.

This is Burnham’s first test as Prime Minister, and maybe he will learn from it.

Maybe he will learn that the Ministry of Justice is full of people who are wildly incompetent and have made careers out of failing upwards.



In their advice to him in this case, they have failed spectacularly.

The party line is that the exemption of PC Harper’s killers is impossible.

Yet no one has explained why it would be impossible to pass primary legislation to exempt those convicted of the ­manslaughter of police officers.

Similar legislation has been created to detain ­terrorists in the past.



Are we saying that the apparatus of the state is unable to fix this problem?

Rather than listening to advisers who are trying to protect their reputations, ­Burnham should be listening to the police officers who have been left demoralised.

He should be listening to PC Harper’s family, and thousands of other victims who are faced with the agony of not knowing whether or not the perpetrators of crimes against them will soon be back walking the streets.

And yet this is not the first time a ­failure to tackle prison system issues has derailed a Prime Minister in the early days of their premiership.

Just two months after he was sworn in in July 2024, Keir Starmer saw criminals popping champagne corks outside ­Wandsworth Prison as they celebrated their early release under his scheme to ease prison overcrowding.



The embarrassing episode came when the new PM was still finding his feet, and some would say he never recovered from it.

Which begs the question: When will politicians learn that draining confidence in the prison system is electoral ­kryptonite?

Clearly Burnham is not a ­student of recent history.



His response may be that Labour ­inherited this mess from the ­Conservative government, and that they have “no choice” but to act as our prisons are fast approaching full capacity.

While I suspect the Ministry of Justice projections may overestimate the speed at which this is happening, we do of course have an urgent problem with prison ­overcrowding in this country.

In my view, the only way to deal with this is with the rapid expansion of the prison estate — which is possible, if not ­palatable.

In recent years, statistics show the ­number of female inmates is down. Releasing 40 per cent of these — ­excluding those in for violent and/or sexual offences — would free up hundreds of spaces.

Removing non-violent criminals who have offended due to drug addiction to secure NHS detox facilities could free up as many as 5,000 places.



Existing prisons which have been closed down, such as HMP Dartmoor and HMP Camp Hill, could also be used to create headroom.

The helpless inability to ­mobilise the enormous resources of the state to create additional space is woeful.

And there are further options which could be explored.

In 1997, the Labour government introduced HMP Weare — a ship moored in Portland Harbour — to ease overcrowding.

Before its closure in 2005, it held 400 inmates who consistently said the ­conditions on board were better than in prisons like Brixton.



There are no easy options here.

But if Burnham is to survive this first test, he needs to stop listening to the usual suspects in the prison reform ­system who were responsible for telling him that keeping Albert Bowers and Jessie Cole in prison was “impossible”.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Instead, he needs to start listening to the public — who have, to date, left almost a ­million signatures on a petition for the killers to remain caged.

And he needs to listen to the frontline police officers who leave home each ­morning knowing that — like PC Harper — they may not come back.­

News.title: Andy Burnham should stop lecturing Brits on illegal migrants and actually come up with plan to stop mega-dinghies
News.content:
Stop the boasts

ANDY Burnham’s reaction to public fury at illegal migrants being housed in their communities spoke volumes.

“I believe all parts of the country need to work, to play their part,” he said.



His suggestion that every area must accommodate asylum seekers who leave France entirely misses the point.

It’s not a question of families playing their part.



Those tens of thousands of incomers — many of them young men, some of whom will pose a public danger — should NOT be here in the first place.

Burnham’s astonishingly tin-eared plea came just hours after Angela Rayner wrongly suggested most migrants were vulnerable women and children. They just don’t get it.

An illegal migrant is currently landing on our shores EVERY 14 MINUTES.

Instead of lecturing the public on their responsibilities, how about Burnham gets round to holding an emergency Cobra meeting on the mega-dinghies?

All we’ve had so far is ministers boasting about cutting the number of asylum hotels when they are dumping migrants in Houses of Multiple Occupation.

Or the Government claiming to have cut crossings by 40 per cent when it’s widely acknowledged that the weather remains the only reliable way of stopping the boats.



Where is the Rwanda-style deterrent that was showing signs it could work before Labour foolishly axed it? Where is the action on ending free housing and benefits for asylum seekers?

What, Prime Minister, is the plan?

In a right state

KEIR Starmer once bemoaned the Civil Service for sitting in the tepid bath of managed decline.

It seems under a new Prime Minister that the temperature has dropped another few degrees.

Whitehall’s response to prison overcrowding has been inept.



Their “can’t do” attitude has forced a disastrous early release scheme that the Chief Inspector of Prisons says could inflict a wave of rape and murder.

Is it any wonder we see so much state uselessness when the majority of civil servants can swap working at their desks for sitting at home in the sunshine?

Keep it down

CHANCELLOR John Healey says his ­number one mission is to ease the cost of living for families.

There is one surefire way to do just that: Scrap the 5p fuel duty increase due to kick in on January 1.

So far, Andy Burnham has been happy to spend billions to knock £45 off energy bills or a quid off bus fares.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

Keeping pump prices down would put a bit more money back in the family coffers and help to rein in food prices.

That’s how to make a REAL difference.

News.title: Tate brothers’ multiple passports under bizarre aliases are unearthed – including Bond villain
News.content:
ALLEGED rapists Andrew and Tristan Tate had held several passports under different aliases – including one name borrowed from a Bond villain.

Court documents show Tristan Tate held a Mexican passport with his photo and date of birth, but a mysterious different name.



The passport was under the name “Vladimir Scorpius” – the eponymous villain of the 007 spy novel “Scorpius”, court documents show.

Tristan also posted an online video declaring “I’m Vladimir Scorpius” and registered a UK company called “Scorpius Ltd.” in reference to the fictional arms dealer from the 1988 novel by John Gardner.



Meanwhile, Andrew Tate openly bragged on social media about having “8 lives … 8 licenses and passports,” and evading authorities in multiple countries, according to the documents.

Prosecutors also claim Andrew was in possession of a stash of travel documents from the UK, US, Estonia, Nigeria, Poland and the Pacific island nation of Vanuatu.

The shocking details about the manosphere influencers‘ series of identities were revealed in new filings from the British Embassy in Washington this week in the Southern District of Florida.

The embassy is currently fighting the brothers’ bid to be released on bond as they seek to avoid extradition to the UK.



The filing warns they pose a flight risk, citing dozens of post by Andrew that “demonstrate that he has access to multiple passports, and that he is willing to use false identities to evade law enforcement”.

In one video, Andrew claimed if he was stopped by police, he would simply “pull out a licence from some random country” to hide his real identity.

British prosecutors also allege there is “substantial grounds to believe that Andrew Tate and Tristan Tate would attempt to identify and interfere with witnesses if released”.

Andrew Tate, 39, and his brother Tristan, 38, were arrested at a bare-knuckle boxing event in Miami on July 18.

They are currently being held in secure housing in federal detention.



Andrew described his Special Housing Unit (SHU) as “punitive housing for people who murder their cellmates“.

He also claimed he was staying in “the worst possible conditions the US gov provides to terrorists and psychopaths”, before adding the inmate in the neighbouring cell was a “cannibal who screams throughout the night”.

His only water source, he complains, is a shower and a “brown and filthy faucet” which has left him suffering “persistent stomach problems”.

In another message on X, Andrew woefully claimed he had “no commissary. No visits. No contact with the outside world.”

“I am an innocent until proven guilty extradition detainee. I’m wanted by a foreign state. I am an American citizen. WHY AM I HERE?” he demanded.



The brothers are fighting extradition to the UK, where they face a total of 59 criminal charges, including rape, sex trafficking and offenses related to indecent images of a child and extreme pornography.

A detention hearing has been scheduled for Thursday.

British prosecutors say these latest charges were fast-tracked after authorities investigated claims made by another four victims.

These new claims are part of a long-running international legal battle involving the Tates, spaning across the US, Britain and Romania.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

The pair are being criminally prosecuted over allegations which include having sex with a minor, trafficking minors, running an organised crime operation and money laundering.



Andrew and Tristan have denied all charges against them.

News.title: Perseid meteor shower live: Watch shooting stars after solar eclipse in 'best night of year'
News.content:
A meteor shower will delight those who stay up, scientists say

After a dramatic solar eclipse wowed millions, another amazing astronomical event is taking place in the skies above us tonight - something scientists call the 'one of the best nights of year'

A dramatic meteor shower is set to put on a show just hours after millions of Brits were wowed by the solar eclipse.

The Perseid meteor shower will be visible from midnight until dawn on Thursday (August 13). Meteor showers occur when the Earth moves through space surrounded by comets breaking up.

It's thought to be the first time in the world the peak of a shower has coincided with a solar eclipse, prompting some scientists to say it's the 'best night of the year' in astronomy. Alfredo Carpineti, space and physics editor at IFL Science and author of the book Invisible Rainbows, said: "It's so exciting to have these two events happening on the same day.

"I've gone through 5,000 years' worth of eclipse data from NASA, and it looks like Wednesday will be the first time there's an eclipse happening on the same day as the peak of a major meteor shower."

Astronomers say it's best to view the shower from a dark countryside hill, where up to 100 comets an hour will be visible.

This is a live event. Please check below for the latest updates.

News.title: 'When doctors say they're struggling - we should listen'
News.content:
'When doctors say they're struggling - we should listen'

"These are professionals being asked to work under relentless pressure in a health service still stretched by staff shortages, rising demand and exhausting workload"

View Image Voice of the Mirror has its say...

When doctors say they are struggling to give patients the care they need, we should all pay attention.

‌



More than four in ten GPs say this happens at least once a week. Among them, the figure rises to a deeply worrying 60 per cent.

‌



These are not medics who have suddenly lost their dedication. They are professionals being asked to work under relentless pressure in a health service still stretched by staff shortages, rising demand and exhausting workloads.

‌



The consequences are felt on both sides of the consulting-room door. Patients wait longer, doctors burn out and more experienced staff begin to wonder whether they can carry on.

The fact that more than one in five doctors are now considering leaving the profession for reasons other than retirement should alarm ministers. Britain cannot build a stronger NHS while the people expected to deliver it are being pushed towards the exit.

Doctors need the time, staff and support to do what they entered medicine to do: care properly for patients.

‌



Time to adapt

Britain’s latest heatwave is becoming a warning about how vulnerable the country is to a changing climate.

The power grid is under pressure. Trains are being cancelled. Firefighters are battling wildfires, reservoirs are shrinking, and 45 million people are living in drought-hit areas.

Tomorrow could bring 38C temperatures and a rise in heat-related deaths. Each problem can be explained away on its own.

‌



Taken together, they paint a far more troubling picture of a nation whose infrastructure was built for a climate that is disappearing. Extreme heat is no longer an occasional inconvenience. It is testing our railways, energy supplies, water reserves and emergency services at the same time.

Britain must adapt faster, because summers like this are becoming harder to dismiss as exceptional. Each of us must play a part.

Eclipse

For a few minutes, the country stopped and looked up.

Article continues below

Streets fell quiet while families and friends gathered outside as the solar eclipse shrouded the nation in darkness.

In a country too often pulled apart by division, millions shared the same breathtaking sight together. For once, we were all looking the same way.

News.title: Families of road crash victims share harrowing failures as damning report demands change
News.content:
Families of road crash victims share harrowing failures as damning report demands change

Families who lost loved ones in road crashes have called for action after a report by the Victims' Commissioner for England and Wales, Claire Waxman, warned they are routinely let down

View 3 Images John Liddle, pictured with wife Louise, died after being knocked off his bike by a minibus in Gateshead in 2023 (Image: Louise Liddle)

Heartbroken families who lost loved ones in road crashes have described harrowing failures as a damning report warned road crime is not treated as seriously as it should be.

‌



A damning report said loved ones of those killed, as well as seriously injured survivors, are routinely left in limbo and without proper support. A study by the Victims' Commissioner for England and Wales warned poor communication, lengthy police investigations, court delays and difficulties accessing support mean those affected face further injustice.

‌



In the year to June 2025, 1,579 people died on roads, while over 25,000 were seriously injured. Joan and Mike O’Connor, whose 20-year-old son Liam died after being hit by a taxi on a pedestrian crossing in 2023, said: "After losing our child in such a devastating and traumatic manner, you’d think nothing else can be as bad. But our experience of the criminal justice system heaped layer after layer of injustice upon us and re-traumatised us at every stage.”

‌



Newcastle University student Liam, an academy player at Sale Sharks rugby union club, died from his injuries. No charges were brought against the driver following a 15-month police investigation.

Disposable barbeques could be banned to help prevent wildfire risk, Andy Burnham says READ MORE :

Andy Burnham responds to heartbreaking plea by PC Andrew Harper's sister READ MORE :

View 3 Images Student Liam O'Connor died after being hit by a taxi in Newcastle (Image: Family Handout )

Liam’s parents, Joan and Mike, say that throughout the lengthy investigation and inquest process they felt desperately let down, shut out, and re-traumatised. They said they were stunned when ambulance footage was shown during Liam's inquest with no warning.

‌



The couple said: “We should have been given the choice whether we wanted to see the video from the start, but we weren’t. The experience was completely re-traumatising." No charge was ever brought in relation to Liam's death following a 15 month police investigation.

Joan and Mike said in a statement: “If our fit, healthy 20-year-old son had died in any other circumstance, such as a drunken punch while still inside the pub that night, we believe the response of the CPS (Crown Prosecution Service) would have been completely different. Instead, victims of road collisions are treated like second-class victims."

Louise Liddle, whose 44-year-old husband John died after being knocked off his bike by a minibus in 2023, said: "Victims don't just suffer because of the incident itself. They suffer because of the uncertainty, the delays and the lack of trauma-informed support afterwards. We should not have to become campaigners to fix the system.”

‌



She said that while John was in a coma, she felt let down by the criminal justice system. Louise recalled: “I felt the police were on my side throughout and were genuinely fighting for my case. They appealed the CPS’s decision not to prosecute the bus driver twice.

View 3 Images Victims' Commissioner Claire Waxman said the government must act

"But so much is out of their control because protocols limit what action they can take and what information they can share. In my case, red tape meant the police weren’t able to interview the bus driver for nineweeks, and they didn’t have the power to suspend his driving licence pending the outcome of the investigation.

‌



"So, he returned to work straight away, driving minibuses past my house every day. That was incredibly traumatic and I had to move away from the area as a result."

The report said there must be stronger oversight and accountability for road traffic collision investigations. It also called for police to be given consistent training for dealing with traumatised families, and fund specialist road traffic collision victim support services.

Claire Waxman, Victims’ Commissioner for England and Wales, said: “Behind every road death or serious injury is a victim, a grieving family and lives changed forever. Yet too many victims told me they felt road crime was not treated with the seriousness it deserved and that the harm they had suffered mattered less than other serious crimes.

Article continues below

“Many spoke of lengthy investigations, poor communication, repeated delays and a lack of support at the very time they needed it most. Some were forced to fight for basic information, answers and recognition while trying to cope with unimaginable loss and trauma.

“These experiences are not inevitable." Ross Moorlock, chief executive of road safety charity Brake, said: “The report makes a compelling case for a more victim-centred approach, with timely and thorough investigations, stronger national standards, trauma-informed practice across all victim-facing agencies, and sustainable funding for specialist support services.”

News.title: Solar eclipse wows UK and Europe in once-in-a-generation display - dramatic images
News.content:
The first near-total solar eclipse visible from the UK since 1999 has given skygazers a night to remember with a total eclipse then wowing Spain and Portugal

A once-in-a-generation solar eclipse has stunned skygazers across the UK and Europe as pictures and video emerge of the spectacular event at its peak.

The celestial show saw the Moon slide in front of the Sun in the UK's first near-total solar eclipse in more than half a century. In Europe a spectacular total eclipse drew massive crowds in Spain and Portugal.

Van Sabellina, 31, from Truro, was among those watching the eclipse at Land's End in Cornwall - one of the places that saw the highest percentage of the Sun blocked out.

She said: "It was amazing - once in a lifetime. We were very lucky with the weather and being able to witness it in Land’s End was just spectacular. It was a bit eerie - you feel the change in temperature from hot to refreshing and cold."

Kim Rebecca, 26, watched the eclipse from Greenwich Park, south east London, and said it was "an amazing phenomenon". She said: "It is still hot but it is noticeably cooler than it was.

"You would normally think it would be quieter when it happened but, maybe because it is south east London, there was champagne corks popping."

The next eclipse in the UK is coming in August next year - you can read our complete list of eclipses that will be visible in the coming years here.

News.title: 'Nigel Farage’s £250,000 Clacton by-election stunt cannot make the investigation disappear'
News.content:
'Nigel Farage’s £250,000 Clacton by-election stunt cannot make the investigation disappear'

"For a man who has built a career denouncing waste in Westminster and Whitehall, the contradiction is glaring, with the cost of polling stations, staff, security and a count of ballot papers"

View Image Voice of the Mirror has its say...

Nigel Farage has for years won support by selling himself as the taxpayer’s watchdog, hunting down waste and making Westminster answer for every penny.

‌



On Thursday, that collides with reality as the people of Clacton go back to the polls in a by-election costing around £250,000 of vital public money, despite electing him as their MP only two years ago. There was no death, no boundary change, no scandal serious enough to force him out. Just Farage’s decision to resign.

‌



Farage has always understood the power of the outsider, the man who says ­that ­politicians live by one set of rules while ordinary people live by another. But accountability has to apply when the scrutiny lands on you.

‌



The Reform UK leader walked away while Parliament’s standards watchdog was investigating his failure to declare a £5million gift from Thai cryptocurrency billionaire Christopher Harborne. His explanation for that money has shifted more than once: security costs, a reward for Brexit, then simply cash he was free to spend as he pleased.

Farage denies wrongdoing, and no finding has been made against him so far. Those facts matter.

‌



So does another: when Farage stopped being an MP, the investigation stopped with him. If he returns to ­Parliament, it can begin again.

That is what makes this election so hard to justify. Farage could have remained representing the people who elected him, and let the process reach its conclusion.

For a man who has built a career denouncing waste in Westminster and Whitehall, the contradiction is glaring. There’s the cost of polling stations, staff, security and a count of ballot papers with a record 34 candidates.

Article continues below

We already know the script if Farage wins: Clacton has spoken, the establishment has been defeated, Reform is unstoppable. The trouble is, none of the major parties have fielded a candidate.

Farage may win handsomely, but one needless by-election does not prove the country has embraced him as its next Prime Minister.

This is bigger than Count Binface, a giant ballot paper or the circus gathered around this election. It is about the standards we demand from people who seek power.

News.title: Nigel Farage slopes off to battle with a bin in Clacton by-election farce as stunt backfires
News.content:
Nigel Farage slopes off to battle with a bin in Clacton by-election farce as stunt backfires

With his popularity on the slide and mired in a donor scandal, Nigel Farage’s political career could fall into the shadows even if he wins his by-election stunt

View 5 Images It's Bin Day in Clacton and Nigel Farage risks being eclipsed by Count Binface

Brits gazed in wonder at the eclipse ­yesterday… as shadows fell across Nigel Farage’s chances of ever becoming PM ahead of Thursday's humiliating battle with Count Binface.

The Reform leader forced a by-election in Clacton and avoided an investigation into his £5million gift from a crypto-billionaire. But with a reinvigorated Labour now ahead in the polls under new leader Andy Burnham, Farage faces two outcomes.

He either wins and the probe into his finances continues. Or he loses to a bin.

View 5 Images Count Binface is expected to lose in Clacton (Image: James Veysey/Shutterstock)

With his popularity on the slide and mired in a donor scandal, Mr Farage’s political career could fall into the shadows even if he wins his by-election stunt. Voters head to the ballot box in Clacton on Thursday for a contest that the Reform UK leader thought would end the scrutiny into his financial affairs.

Facing a Parliamentary Standards Commissioner probe over a £5million gift, he quit to trigger a poll that could cost taxpayers £250,000. But if he beats the selection of comedy ­candidates he is up against – after the main parties boycotted the farce – the questions about donations will continue.

And his task has been made even more ­difficult by new Prime Minister Andy Burnham, whose series of interventions to make life easier for struggling Brits has seen Labour pull ahead of Reform in the polls.

Instead of an MP who fights for their interests, voters in Clacton must choose between a ­candidate with laughable policies only running for their own ego, or Count Binface.

In a sign of how ridiculous the race has become, Rob Pownall, who has previously fought campaigns dressed as a fox to raise awareness of animal welfare, dropped out saying the by-election was too silly.

Burnham's bold moves

During a summer which Mr Farage has spent arguing with a bin, the PM has capped bus fares, slashed energy bills and cut hospitality rates for pubs. After giving families some much-needed breathing space, Mr Burnham unveiled a huge devolution shake-up – allowing local leaders to keep more of the cash residents pay and invest it back into their communities.

In a positive vision for Britain, he has also promised an end to rough sleeping, vowed to transform social care and pledged to give locals a greater say over new shops that can open to help revitalise high streets.

Meanwhile Mr Farage has unveiled ill-thought out ideas such as returning migrant boats using the Navy, something France has said would violate its sovereignty and breach international law. He also pledged to send foreign prisoners to El Salvador, an idea branded unworkable by Labour and dismissed by former Tory minister Ben Wallace, who accused Reform of lying.

View 5 Images Farage stepped down as an MP last month (Image: Dinendra Haria/SOPA Images/Shutterstock)

Despite this, Mr Farage is the favourite to wake up on Friday having won the by-election – but that does nothing to end the sleaze probe into the £5m he received from crypto-billionaire Christopher Harborne. Mr Farage did not declare the sum, insisting he did not need to – despite rules stating donations and political gifts in the 12 months before entering Parliament must be made public.

Becoming rattled over questions about the cash, he lashed out on LBC, claiming it was “none of your business”, before boasting: “I can spend it on Ferraris if I want.” That probe is set to resume if Mr Farage wins. If he is found to have breached rules, he could face a suspension, potentially sparking yet another by-election.

View 5 Images Andy Burnham has heaved Labour back to the top of the polls (Image: Getty Images)

On Mr Farage’s by-election stunt, polling guru Sir John Curtice said: “So far it hasn’t paid off.

“The calling of the by-election and the events immediately pertaining to that do seem to have done Reform a certain amount of damage. His personal popularity has gone down a bit as well.”

Sir John said by-election rules have also hindered Mr Farage on the national stage.

He explained: “Because of the absence of candidates from the main parties, it has been quite difficult for the broadcasters to put him on air, because if you put him on, who else do you put on air? It has arguably reduced his national visibility, rather than served to increase it.”

View 5 Images Nigel Farage has been damaged by the by-election, Sir John Curtice claimed (Image: James Manning/PA Wire)

Article continues below

He added that Reform would not just be worried about Labour, but that the Tories were also “breathing down Reform’s neck”.

Dismissing the by-election, Bridget Phillipson MP, Chair of the Labour Party, said: “The only thing we’ll learn from bin day is that Nigel Farage can waste the people of Clacton’s time.

“This by-election stunt has failed to distract from the scandal and sleaze surrounding Farage and Reform. He needs to start answering questions about why he failed to declare a £5m gift.”

News.title: Solar eclipse eye damage urgent warning as expert lists symptoms to look out for
News.content:
Solar eclipse eye damage urgent warning as expert lists symptoms to look out for

The solar eclipse was a spectacular event, but eye health experts warn of a genuine risk of solar retinopathy for those who looked directly at it without protection

View 2 Images The eclipse seen from Southend on Sea (Image: Martin Dalton/Shutterstock)

Thousands of skygazers across the UK and the world have been treated to a breathtaking solar eclipse, with eye health specialists urging people to watch the spectacle through certified protective eyewear.

‌



The Moon passed directly between the Earth and the Sun, blocking out the Sun's face in a historic moment - the most significant eclipse since 1999.

‌



Experts have now issued stark warnings about the dangers facing those who stared directly at the eclipse without the right protection.

‌



Despite being a partial eclipse, specialists caution that there is a very real risk to eye health for anyone who attempted to view it with the naked eye.

Nkosi Yearwood, optometrist and The College of Optometrists council member for Wales said: "People often forget that the sun gives out a lot more light than just visible light. There are also ultraviolet rays, infrared rays, and it's this whole spectrum that is harmful to our eyes."

View 2 Images (Image: Liverpool Echo)

‌



"Because the sun starts dimming in the eclipse, many people think that it's safe to look at, but actually even if it's a 90% coverage, you've still got 10% of the sun that you're staring at, and that's still a lot of energy."

How can looking directly at the solar eclipse without certified filters impact your eyes?

"If you look directly at it, it can cause damage to the back of the eye and can cause some retinopathy," Patrick Laidlaw, an optometrist based at Optegra Eye Clinic Sheffield said. "If you look at it for too long you could even develop a central bit of field loss."

This is because looking directly at a solar eclipse can affect the macula.

‌



"There's a point at the back of the eye called the macula, which is where you get your central vision from, and it's highly populated with photoreceptors. Intense light can cause toxicity and can essentially burn the back of the eye," explains Laidlaw.

Yearwood points out that historical evidence suggests this damage can occur even after only a brief glance.

"In the days following the last eclipse in the Nineties, around 70 people across the UK presented to eye departments with some level of solar retinopathy, and about 40% of these people looked at it for less than a minute."

‌



What red flag eye symptoms should we look out for?

Symptoms typically tend to be delayed. "It can take a few hours or even couple of days before you start feeling the symptoms," says Yearwood.

He said that many people fail to notice anything immediately, as there is generally no pain associated with the condition.

"The retina doesn't have any pain receptors, so you can do this damage and not know about it," says Yearwood.

‌



Nevertheless, there are other warning signs to be aware of, ranging from mild to severe. "The main things to look out for is any blurring in vision, distortion, a dark spot or a change in your colour vision," says Yearwood.

"If you experience any of these symptoms or just feel like things aren't quite right, seek advice from an optometrist at your local opticians straight away."

Laidlaw adds: "I would also look out for any severe light sensitivity or any reduction in vision."

‌



What do optometrists look for?

"We look for any changes to the macular region, because that's the part of your eye which focuses on the very fine detail. Whenever you're looking at something, your macula is focused on it, and we tend to see changes to the retinal cells," says Yearwood. "It generally shows up as a yellowish spot."

Can this damage be treated or reversed?

There is no treatment for it, but it can heal itself. "Similar to sunburn, it does in most cases does heal itself," says Yearwood.

"The length of time to heal and how high the chance of healing depends on how long you look at the eclipse for.

Article continues below

"So, if you did end up staring at it for too long, you do risk permanent vision damage. If you are worried, go to your local opticians and let them assess you."

News.title: Solar eclipse chaos as police called to tackle crowds rushing for free glasses
News.content:
Solar eclipse chaos as police called to tackle crowds rushing for free glasses

Hundreds of people descended on a tent in Bristol's Sea Walls handing out free glasses ahead of today's once-in-a-lifetime solar eclipse

View Image (Image: Tom Wren / SWNS)

Police were forced to intervene earlier today after hundreds of people swarmed a tent in Bristol handing out free eclipse glassed.

‌



A crowd descended on a stand hosted by science centre We The Curious at the city's Sea Walls earlier today, as they sought to hand out free glasses ahead of today's partial solar eclipse.

‌



But the demand soon spiralled out of control, and before long police were called to manage the queue at the Sea Walls as people tried to secure their glasses for the once-in-a-lifetime event. One eyewitness at the scene said some people grew unruly when they were unable to get their glasses.

‌



Due to there being no parking at the Sea Walls, vehicles were also double and triple-parked on the grass, they added.

The South West boasts one of the best spots in the entire country to view the eclipse, which began just after 6pm, with maximum eclipse, when the sun is most obscured, taking place around an hour later at just after 7pm.

One onlooker described the thousands of people flocking to view the rare astrological event as "a scene from Independence Day," BristolLive reported.

‌



Millions of people across the country witnessed the most dramatic partial eclipse seen in the UK since 1999, which saw over 90% of the surface eclipsed by the moon.

Crowds of people could be seen at viewing spots in different locations – including the Royal Observatory Greenwich, London, Calton Hill, Edinburgh, and outside Queen’s University in Belfast on Wednesday evening.

Speaking at the UK’s largest space attraction in Leicester, Dhara Patel, who is a space expert at the National Space Centre, said some people may be overcome by emotion while watching the eclipse.

‌



“For a lot of people, it can be a little bit of an emotional event," she said.

“I’ve seen previously people being drawn to tears or just have a really good moment within themselves where they realise they’re seeing or witnessing something… you’ve never seen before in your life.”

She described it as “incredible” to be able to witness this eclipse, adding: “We’ve had solar eclipses over the last couple of years, about 30% coverage.

‌



“They’ve been good, but this is definitely a different scale.

“And what’s really nice is it’s a way for lots of people to come together and connect with nature – looking up at the sky at objects that we typically tend to take for granted.”

The Royal Greenwich Observatory said it had sold approximately 15,000 pairs of eclipse glasses, a sellout, in the last month.

‌



John Lewis said colander sales have increased nearly 40% compared to last year, as Nasa recommends the kitchen item as a way to watch the eclipse by viewing the shadows it casts on the ground.

A spokesperson said: “Colander sales have surged nearly 40% compared to last year, as shoppers prepare for tonight’s eclipse.

“We’ve still got plenty of stock for anyone wanting to view this solar phenomenon safely, and, unlike eclipse glasses, you can use it to strain your spaghetti for dinner afterwards.”

Article continues below

News.title: Once-in-a-generation solar eclipse wows millions in UK and Europe
News.content:
The UK and Europe have enjoyed their most dramatic solar eclipse for nearly 30 years, with millions thought to have witnessed the once-in-a-generation event.

Those watching the astronomical phenomenon from the UK were treated to a partial eclipse, which peaked shortly after 19:00 BST, when most saw more than 90% of the Sun covered by the Moon.

But parts of Greenland, Iceland and Spain experienced the complete darkness and spectacle of a total eclipse.

Large crowds at viewing sites across the UK and Europe reacted with gasps and cheers, with astronomy enthusiasts saying it served as a reminder of how "amazing" the universe is.

News.title: Millions watch 'surreal' solar eclipse in UK and Europe
News.content:
Millions of people across Europe and the UK witnessed the most significant solar eclipse since 1999 on Wednesday.

For the UK, more than 90% of the Sun was covered by the Moon, whereas in some parts of Europe, a rare total eclipse could be seen.

BBC science correspondent Pallab Ghosh was in Burgos, Spain, and said he got goosebumps from the spectacle.

News.title: Students wait for A-level, T-level and BTec results
News.content:
Hundreds of thousands of students in England, Wales and Northern Ireland will receive A-level, T-level and BTec results on Thursday morning.

Another record number of students are expected to find out they have secured a place at their first choice of university.

The cost of going to university has been in the spotlight this year, with mounting pressure on the government to reform student loan repayments, and there has been a renewed focus on technical education under Prime Minister Andy Burnham.

But the chief executive of Universities UK, which represents more than 140 vice-chancellors, urged students to not "let politicians make your decision for you".

About 40% of 18-year-olds in England receive A-levels every summer.

Around 250,000 grades for vocational and technical qualifications are also expected to be released to students in England, including BTec National, Cambridge Technical, Cambridge Advanced National and T-level results.

AS-levels, which will count towards students' final A-level results next summer in Wales and Northern Ireland, will also be released.

This year, the pass rate for National 5, Higher and Advanced Higher exams in Scotland rose across the board.

And last year, the proportion of students getting top A-level results reached a record high, with 28.3% of all grades across England, Wales and Northern Ireland marked at A* or A.

News.title: Double killer and rapist given whole life sentence
News.content:
A serial sex attacker who had a "morbid fascination" with sex has been jailed for the rest of his life after he was found guilty of murdering two women and raping a third.

Simon Levy, 40, killed Carmenza Valencia-Trujillo, 53, in March 2025 and 39-year-old Sheryl Wilkins five months later. Earlier that year, he raped a third woman in the same Tottenham car park where Wilkins was later found dead.

At the Old Bailey on Wednesday, Judge Mark Lucraft KC sentenced Levy to a whole life order, meaning he will never be released.

The sentence comes after police and the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) apologised over a series of disastrous decisions that left him free to roam the streets.

When Levy carried out the attacks, he was on bail and being monitored by the Met.

The police watchdog is currently examining how he was managed over a four-year period, from his first conviction in September 2021 for sexual assault up to his final arrest in September 2025.

Following Wednesday's sentencing, Met Police Commissioner Sir Mark Rowley said the handling of Levy's case was a "whole system failing".

News.title: Burnham urges shops not to sell disposable BBQs over wildfire risks
News.content:
Andy Burnham has urged shops to stop selling disposable barbecues amid increased wildfire risk driven by this summer's droughts.

The prime minister said he was urging "all retailers big and small" to adhere to voluntary guidance to suspend sales during extreme heat.

He added that in the "longer term" the government would look at potentially banning the single-use grills during summer months.

It comes after a potential ban was discussed at an emergency Cobra meeting on the government's response to record temperatures.

A number of large retailers and supermarkets have voluntarily stopped selling the devices under a framework, external agreed in 2023 between fire chiefs and the British Retail Consortium (BRC).

This says that retailers should suspend sales once an extreme heat event has been declared as imminent, or in response to "reasonable, evidence based" requests from local councils.

Earlier, Burnham told reporters single-use grills had been behind a number of recent blazes and people should not be using them "at this moment in time".

"We do want people to take the greatest possible care when they are out in the countryside, both in terms of cigarettes, but also those temporary barbecues that we know are causing risk of fires."

After the Cobra meeting, Burnham said: "We would say to retailers do not put disposable barbecues on sale at this moment in time."

Nearly three-quarters of England and all of Wales have been officially declared in drought, creating conditions rife for fire to spread.

The Met Office has issued a rare amber extreme heat warning for Thursday, with temperatures peaking in the mid-to-high 30s across the Midlands and south-east of England, and a high of 38C possible.

News.title: GB's Hudson-Smith wins historic 400m gold on home track
News.content:
On his childhood track, in front of a stand named in his honour, hometown hero Matthew Hudson-Smith was not going to be denied.

A full-circle moment, completed by writing his name in history.

More than two decades after stepping foot inside Alexander Stadium for the first time aged nine, Hudson-Smith delivered Great Britain's latest gold in Birmingham to become the joint-most decorated man of all-time at European Championships.

The 31-year-old celebrated the third European 400m title of his illustrious career by making his way into the crowd and placing a hand on the banner bearing his name.

Moments before, Hudson-Smith had stormed down the home straight, just as he had countless times before as a member of local club Birchfield Harriers.

This time, though, the Olympic and world silver medallist did so to rapturous cheers inside the arena which fostered his love for the sport.

With his eighth podium at the championships, Hudson-Smith equalled French sprinter Christophe Lemaitre's men's record medal tally - with the relays still to come.

"Honestly, words can't describe how much that meant to me," he told BBC Sport.

"Nobody was going to beat me on this track. This is my home. I know this track like the back of my hand. I have my stand. Now I'm going to go for Mayor of Birmingham and Wolverhampton!

"I knew I was the best in the world. I knew that, on paper, I was a second faster than every single one of these guys. It was about me and the clock."

News.title: Eurovision Song Contest changes rules for countries at war
News.content:
Organisers of the Eurovision Song Contest have updated their rules to state that if a country involved in an armed conflict wins the competition, it will be ineligible to host it the following year.

The amendment was approved by the contest's governing body, following feedback from participating broadcasters after Eurovision 2026 in Vienna.

It states that winning countries will also be disqualified from hosting if a "sensitive geopolitical situation" affects the "security, safety or stability of their state or immediate region".

The update will be interpreted as a reaction to Israel's continued presence at the contest, amid criticism of its military actions in Gaza and the Middle East.

Last November, following a failed attempt to have Israel suspended, five broadcasters announced they were boycotting the competition - including Eurovision powerhouses Spain and Ireland.

Despite the protests, Israel's Noam Bettan ultimately took second place with his song Michelle.

It marked the second year in a row that Israel had taken the runners-up position - and some participating broadcasters have privately expressed safety concerns over the contest being staged in Jerusalem or Tel Aviv, should the country win in the future.

Although Israel will undoubtedly be seen as the target of the rule change, it will also affect Ukraine, which has been engaged in a protracted war since it was invaded by Russia in 2022.

Ukrainian group Kalush Orchestra went on to win Eurovision that same year, in a symbolic show of public support.

Following their victory, Eurovision organisers undertook a "full assessment and feasibility study" to decide whether the 2023 contest could proceed in Kyiv.

They ultimately decided the security risks were too great, and the UK stepped in to host the competition in Liverpool.

News.title: First 100% British chocolate bar made since 1932
News.content:
A chocolate bar has been made using entirely British ingredients for the first time in nearly a century, with cocoa from not Brazil or Bali, but Berkshire.

Created at the University of Reading, it was named the Reading 100 Chocolate Bar to mark the university's 100th anniversary.

It is the first of its kind since 1932, when Rowntree's gifted a six-year-old Princess Elizabeth the only other bar of UK-grown chocolate ever made.

Food security master's student Maha Khan created the chocolate bar by harvesting, fermenting and processing the Reading-grown cocoa.

While the UK's chocolate market is worth Â£10.4bn, it is entirely reliant on imported cocoa.

Maha told the Today programme she made the bar to highlight the challenges facing the cocoa growing industry.

She said: "It is incredible that we can make 100% British chocolate â but in the context of climate change, pests and diseases, there are estimates that 30 to 40% is lost.

"And we've seen with these heatwaves, climate change, these problems and challenges are only going to get exacerbated."

News.title: New Forest wildfire continues as temperatures rise
News.content:
Firefighters on the fourth day of battling a wildfire in the New Forest are facing "challenging" weather conditions with temperatures set to rise again

The blaze began on Sunday 9 August when a van caught fire on the A31, with 23 drivers abandoning their vehicles as the fire took hold.

Hampshire & Isle of Wight Fire and Rescue Service (HIWFRS) said crews had implemented fire breaks and had a 'good hold' of the perimeter of the fire, while changing wind conditions were proving challenging.

National Highways said repairs to the A31 were not expected to be begin until Friday 14 August at the earliest.

News.title: Green councillor charged with assaults
News.content:
A Birmingham Green Party city councillor has been charged with attacking a member of the public, three police officers and a member of police staff.

Siobhan Harper-Nunes, 66, was arrested on suspicion of assault after police were called to the junction of Monument Road and Hagley Road in the city, at about 17:00 BST on Thursday.

Harper-Nunes, of Monument Road, was charged on Friday.

West Midlands Police said that she was arrested again at Monument Road on Wednesday morning on suspicion of harassment.

She remained in custody while inquiries continued, police said.

Harper-Nunes will appear at Birmingham Magistrates' Court on 10 September on the assault charges, the force said.

The councillor was elected in May to represent the Ladywood ward for the city council.

She previously stood as the Green Party's candidate for West Midlands mayor in the 2024 election.

The Birmingham Green Party has been approached for comment.

News.title: Victim of fatal Clapham shooting named
News.content:
A man who was shot dead in south-west London has been named by police as Auguste-Marie Bile-aka Amoa.

Officers and paramedics were called to Willington Road, Clapham, just before 22:00 BST on Monday following reports of gunshots near The Landor pub.

The 25-year-old, who worked as a bus driver, was pronounced dead at the scene, the Metropolitan Police said.

A 22-year-old man was later arrested on suspicion of murder after attending hospital with a gunshot wound on Tuesday. He remains in hospital under police guard.

Det Ch Insp Claire Guiver said her thoughts were with the victim's family as they "come to terms with this tragic incident".

News.title: Ministers push ahead with housing asylum seekers on ex-military sites
News.content:
Home Office minister Anna Turley has said the government is sticking with plans to accommodate asylum-seekers on former military bases despite protests from local residents.

She told the BBC the government's priority was to ensure asylum-seekers were looked after in a "secure" and "appropriate" place.

That included disused Ministry of Defence properties because they had on-site facilities and were "more contained," she added.

But campaigners in areas earmarked for asylum centres have said small communities with limited infrastructure would not be able to cope with large numbers of people.

There have been protests in Piddington, Oxfordshire, over plans to house more than 1,000 asylum seekers at a site near the village.

Mike Nixon, the vice-chairman of Piddington Parish Council, said there was a "huge amount of concern and worry" among residents and that an asylum centre would have a "dramatic effect" on the way they lived their lives.

The proposal has prompted Piddington to hold a symbolic independence referendum, asking its 400 or so residents if they want to remain part of the UK.

Nixon said: "We're still very frustrated. Andy Burnham did say that he's willing to listen, but we've had no formal contact. No consultation, nothing from the Home Office.

"We felt that the only way of making our views felt was to say 'well if we're not going to be listened to, what's the point of being a part of the country?'"

The government has promised to end the use of hotels for asylum seekers, announcing on Wednesday that a further 13 across England had been closed.

It plans to use former military sites instead with two already up and running - RAF Wethersfield in Essex, and Crowborough Training Camp in East Sussex.

In June, it announced proposals to open three more, including the site near Piddington.

The two other planned sites are a former RAF base in Barnham in Suffolk where there were protests last week and RAF Linton-on-Ouse in North Yorkshire where the area's Labour mayor said it was "simply the wrong place".

Defending the proposals on BBC Breakfast, Turley said the public wanted the government to end the use of hotels, pointing to how an "iconic" hotel in Blackpool, the Metropole, was no longer being used to accommodate asylum-seekers.

She said it sent "an important message" that the government wanted the hotel to be part of Blackpool's future.

"The priority is to ensure we look after asylum seekers in a secure place that is more appropriate and we limit the impact on communities."

Asked what she meant by secure, she said: "Examples we are looking at is former military bases and we have two up and running and possibly another three.

"They have have facilities on site and are more contained and it limits the impact on on communities.

"We are looking at other sites such as former industrial sites, student accommodation - accommodation that is more more appropriate than hotels."

News.title: I share concerns over Arday appointment, says Cambridge University head
News.content:
The vice-chancellor of the University of Cambridge has said she understands the concerns raised by the appointment of Jason Arday and shares them too.

In a letter to staff, Prof Deborah Prentice acknowledged the "anger and anxiety around this damaging and difficult case".

The university head also announced Cambridge's investigation would be independent and carried out by senior academics from within and beyond Cambridge and will begin "as soon as possible".

Arday resigned as a Cambridge professor of sociology of education last week amid allegations of plagiarism and questions about some of his achievements.

The 41-year-old - who became Cambridge's youngest ever black professor in 2023 - denies any plagiarism and said the recent furore had led to "an unrelenting level of public scrutiny and personal attack".

In a letter to university staff, Prof Deborah Prentice said: "I fully understand the concerns being raised across the University and well beyond it, regarding Jason Arday's appointment and I share them...

"We will now investigate the circumstances around his appointment by the faculty of education back in 2022 and his time here in Cambridge since his appointment nearly four years ago.

"That investigation, as you say, should be thorough and transparent, and will be carried out independently by senior academics from within and beyond Cambridge."

The findings of the investigation, previously announced on Friday, will inform a review into the process for the appointment of senior academic roles, the university has said.

Prentice added "our staff of colour are highly valued, for their scholarship, their achievements, and the contributions they make" and said the case "should not be used to cast aspersions on their work or the legitimacy of their roles at Cambridge".

Cambridge had previously said allegations of plagiarism regarding Arday's thesis and some journal publications had been investigated by Liverpool John Moores University (LMJU) and the journals in question.

LJMU - which awarded his PhD in 2015 - had investigated the allegations that were made last year, and found he did not commit plagiarism.

In an interview with the Times, Arday defended himself by arguing that he had not received adequate supervision during his PhD given his autism and "learning disabilities".

The University of Cambridge said it had advised people to contact the relevant institution or pass on complaints.

But after Cambridge announced its own investigation, some academics pushed for the inquiry to be independent, questioning whether the university could adequately investigate its own processes.

It is not yet clear how the independent investigation will work or who will lead it. The university said it will look at the circumstances around his appointment by the faculty of education in 2022 and his time in Cambridge since his appointment.

Arday worked as a PE teacher before earning his doctorate at LMJU and going on to become an associate professor at Durham University and professor of sociology of education at the University of Glasgow.

Glasgow has also announced a review into Arday's previous academic post.

When he resigned from his post, Arday said he was not a "liar" and that his resignation "should not be mistaken for an acceptance of the narratives that have surrounded me."

News.title: GB's Evans wins European gold in 100m breaststroke
News.content:
Great Britain's Angharad Evans won her first European Championship gold in the 100m breaststroke final in Paris.

The 23-year-old comfortably finished first in a championship record time of one minute and 4.87 seconds, which was also a lifetime best and British record.

Having also broken the championship record in the semi-final, Evans claimed gold ahead of Ireland's Mona McSharry in second, while Italy's Benedetta Pilato took bronze.

Great Britain's Filip Nowacki, who made history for Jersey by claiming gold in the 200m breaststroke at the Commonwealth Games last month in Glasgow, was the fastest qualifier in the semi-final of the same event at the European Aquatics Championships.

The 18-year-old's time of 2:08.60 held off GB team-mate Greg Butler in the first semi-final, with the 25-year-old also progressing to the final.

GB's Amalie Smith picked up a silver medal in the 400m individual medley final, finishing 0.7secs behind Ireland's Ellen Walshe, with Poland's Justina Kozan claiming bronze.

The 16-year-old Smith, who won gold on Monday in the 4x200m freestyle relay, was also part of the part of the 4x100m freestyle relay team that finished fifth.

Another teenager, Italian Sara Curtis, also shone as she broke the women's 50m backstroke world record with a time of 26.63 seconds.

The 19-year-old bettered the world record set by Australia's Kaylee McKeown three years ago by 0.23secs in her semi-final.

News.title: Man bled to death after being bitten by American XL Bully, court hears
News.content:
A man died from extreme blood loss after suffering "catastrophic injuries" when he was bitten on the leg by an American XL bully in his daughter-in-law's garden, a court has heard.

Keven Jones, 62, from Chester, who was in poor health, taking methadone and blood thinning medication, was staying at Chanel Fong's house at the time of the incident.

The incident took place before XL Bullies were added to the banned dog list in October 2023.

Fong, 33, denies being the owner of the dog, which the prosecution said was dangerously out of control at the time, and also denies an alternative charge of being the person in charge of a dog at the time of the attack.

Opening the case at Caernarfon Crown Court, prosecutor Mark Connor said it was a "sad and tragic case for everyone concerned" and told the jury they would be shown some "graphic images" of Jones' injuries during the trial.

He said it was not a case of whether the XL Bully, named Cookie, was a banned breed, but rather that the dog had been "dangerously out of control" and whether Fong was legally responsible for it, either as its owner or the person responsible for it at the time.

The court was told the dog was owned by Fong and her partner, Joshua Jones, the son of the victim, but that he was not present at the time of the attack.

Connor added that, in her police interview, Fong said on paper Cookie belonged to her partner.

He went on to describe how there were a number of dogs at the property on Holt Road in Wrexham, including Cookie and another XL Bully called Fire, who were in the back garden at the time.

Cookie's mother, an XL Bully called Rogue, was inside the property and was "in season" meaning she had been kept separate from the other dogs in the house.

News.title: Ann Widdecombe's loved ones gather for her funeral
News.content:
Police officers and sniffer dogs were in the grounds of the abbey ahead of the service, which lasted about 90 minutes.

The private requiem mass included a homily from the Rt Rev David Charlesworth, Abbot of Buckfast.

He said: "In the midst of the shock, clamour and sometimes unwarranted comment surrounding her death, our response is to pray for the repose of her soul, to give thanks for her fortitude, and offer Holy Mass in this Abbey Church which Ann called her safe haven."

A statement from the Abbey Church earlier said Widdecombe would be "missed and fondly remembered" and "many in our worshipping community knew her as a kind and warm character".

"Ann was a woman of profound faith, a faith which found expression in the public forum of politics," it said.

It added: "Ann was unafraid to express her unwavering convictions, formed through her Roman Catholic faith. She had a sharp intellect and was a dedicated public servant."

The order of service also included tributes paid by the Rev Roger Widdecombe, Widdecombe's nephew, and Sir Christian Sweeting, a close friend.

A public memorial for Widdecombe is due to be held later this year.

An angler has told of his dramatic escape after he was bitten by a shark off the coast of Ireland.

Sebastian Achim, a content creator from Dungarvan, was reportedly with friends catching blue sharks off the coast of Ardmore, a fishing village in County Waterford on the south coast, on Tuesday when he was attacked.

Mr Achim told All About Cork with Paul Byrne that the shark bit his leg after he pulled it from the water.

“The catch decided to lunge at my leg and grab my calf” he said. “It managed to rip part of my calf and do damage that we required special services for.”

open image in gallery The Irish Coast Guard sent out a helicopter in response and airlifted Mr Achim to hospital (file) ( PA Archive )

Mr Achim said his friends managed to intervene quickly enough to pull the shark off, but he was already fearing for the worst.

“Blood was spraying everywhere ... I knew it was bad ... I was thinking about the damage and I just wanted to get home – actually, I was hoping to get home,” he said.

The Irish Coast Guard in Dublin received a report of the shark attack at 4.16pm on Tuesday, sending out a helicopter from Waterford and two RNLI lifeboats.

Ballycotton RNLI in Cork said it was called by the coast guard to help a “five-metre pleasure craft” with five people on board.

Mr Achim said his friends kept him stable with a makeshift tourniquet and a wrap for the 10cm wound on his leg until the air ambulance arrived and took him to Cork University Hospital.

Doctors were able to treat Mr Achim and save the leg, but he will need further surgeries, according to the Irish Independent.

Ballycotton RNLI coxswain Eolan Walsh said in a statement that the patient “received urgent medical assistance as quickly and safely as possible”.

“Incidents such as this are a reminder that conditions at sea can change quickly and that anyone heading offshore should make safety a priority,” he said, as reported by the BBC.

“Ensure your vessel is suitable for the conditions, wear a properly-fitted lifejacket or personal flotation device, carry a reliable means of communication, and make sure someone ashore knows your plans."

The Independent contacted the RNLI and the Irish coast guard for comment.

The infamous image of President Donald Trump staring directly into the sun during the 2017 solar eclipse has resurfaced - thanks to his own White House - nearly a decade later as another solar eclipse captivated viewers across the U.S. and U.K.

The White House shared the memorable image Wednesday afternoon as millions of people witnessed a once-in-a-generation solar eclipse, which occurs when the Moon passes in front of the sun, creating a bright ring of light around the lunar surface.

People wear solar filters or “eclipse glasses” when taking in the spectacle, since looking straight at the sun, especially during an eclipse, can damage the eyes. Looking at the sun is unsafe except during a brief period of totality, when the moon entirely blocks the sun’s light.

However, that didn’t stop Trump from staring directly at the sky during the August 21, 2017, eclipse.

Trump, who was watching the rare spectacle from the Blue Room Balcony at the White House, was pictured leaning back and looking up at the sky with his eyes uncovered and squinting.

open image in gallery The White House reshared an infamous image of President Donald Trump staring directly into the sun instead of using solar eclipse glasses

The president, then 71, reportedly gesticulated to a crowd of administration staffers gathered below the balcony and pointed to the sky. As he looked up, one of his White House aides then shouted, “Don’t look!” according to a White House pool report from the day.

The moment was immediately dragged on social media — and Trump continued to be trolled and made fun of for it for years to come, as the image resurfacing again in 2024 during another solar eclipse.

The White House’s resharing of the image Wednesday was immediately mocked yet again — while some even shamed the administration for sharing the image, as it may encourage others to participate in the dangerous activity.

“Unlike Trump, Do NOT look directly at the Sun during any phase of a solar eclipse without proper eye protection. Even a few seconds of unprotected viewing can cause solar retinopathy, permanent damage to the retina,” wrote liberal social media influencer Ed Krassenstein.

open image in gallery The image of Trump has been reshared for every solar eclipse since it was taken in 2017 ( AFP/Getty )

“This TWEET is irresponsible and dangerous,” he added.

“The president of the United States is promoting an act that can cause blindness as if it’s a troll. Think about who the intended audience is that might find this amusing. None of them recognize how humiliating this is for America,” another social media user noted.

Others found some humor in the messaging from the White House.

“The White House quote-tweeting NASA with a photo of him ignoring NASA is the whole second term in one image,” one X user wrote.

“Great point that he’s an idiot,” another X user chimed in.

Another social media user simply noted: “Generally not a good idea to try and blind your own supporters.”
