When the MV Barima went down off Guyana on July 18, it looked like a sudden tragedy. Maintenance records tell a slower, harder story: the ferry’s serious faults were documented for months before it sank.

Some of them flagged as urgent.

What happened to the MV Barima

The MV Barima sank on July 18 with 179 people aboard, one of Guyana’s worst recent maritime disasters. By early August, reporting cited 76 people rescued, 72 confirmed dead and 30 still missing.

The scale of loss turned attention quickly to how such a thing could happen.

A paper trail of problems

The most troubling evidence sits in the vessel’s own maintenance records. Logs covering November 2025 to March 2026 describe a string of mechanical failures.

This was not a boat in sudden distress; it was one with a documented history of trouble.

The defects on the list

The records paint a grim picture of the ferry’s condition. They describe an out-of-service generator, overheating machinery, a leaking main-engine exhaust and defective cooling equipment.

Electrical failures also featured, and several entries were marked urgent.

The word that changes everything: ‘urgent’

A defect noted in passing is one thing. A defect marked urgent is another.

It implies someone knew the problem was serious and pressing. That is what turns a maintenance file into a question of accountability.

What is verified, and what is not

It is important to be careful here. The records themselves are documented, and the sinking is beyond dispute.

But whether warnings were deliberately ‘ignored’ depends on who received them and what they decided. That is a question for an official investigation, not a maintenance log alone.

A familiar pattern in transport disasters

Sadly, the shape of this story is common. Many transport tragedies are preceded by documented, unheeded warnings.

Cost, pressure to keep services running and diffuse responsibility often combine. The result is a known risk that is tolerated until it becomes a catastrophe.

Why it matters for Guyana

Guyana is booming on oil wealth, but ferries remain a lifeline for many communities. Public trust in that transport depends on knowing safety is taken seriously.

A disaster tied to ignored defects strikes at that trust directly.

The push for answers

Families of the victims are owed a clear account of what went wrong. An honest inquiry would establish who saw the warnings and why the vessel kept sailing.

Accountability is not only about blame; it is about preventing the next disaster.

What to watch next

The key is the official investigation and whether it confirms the maintenance findings. Also watch for any changes to Guyana’s ferry oversight and inspection rules.

For the families, the priority is simpler: the truth, and that it never happens again.

A lifeline turned deadly

For Guyana’s riverine and coastal communities, ferries are not a convenience but a necessity. They carry people, goods and vehicles where roads simply do not reach.

That dependence is exactly why safety failures on such vessels carry such a heavy human cost.

The oil-wealth contrast

The tragedy lands amid a jarring contrast. Guyana is suddenly one of the world’s fastest-growing economies, thanks to offshore oil.

Yet the everyday infrastructure many citizens rely on has not kept pace with that windfall. A nation earning billions from crude still lost dozens of people on an ageing ferry.

From records to reform

Documented defects are only useful if they drive change. The value of a maintenance log is in acting on it.

Investigators will now ask whether Guyana’s inspection and oversight system failed alongside the vessel. The answer will shape how the country protects passengers in the future.

Frequently Asked Questions

What was the MV Barima?

It was a Guyanese ferry that sank on July 18 with 179 people aboard. In one of the country’s worst recent maritime disasters.

How many people died?

Reporting cited 76 rescued, 72 dead and 30 missing by early August.

What did the records show?

Maintenance logs from November 2025 to March 2026 documented serious defects. Including an out-of-service generator and a leaking engine exhaust, some marked urgent.

Were the warnings ignored?

That specific claim is not yet proven. It depends on who received the reports and chose to keep the vessel sailing, a question for an official inquiry.

Why does it matter?

Ferries are a lifeline in Guyana, and a disaster tied to documented, unheeded faults undermines public trust in transport safety.

Sources: Kaieteur News; Guyanese authorities; local reporting.

World.title: Costa Rica Wildlife Study Records 79 Species at Reserva Conchal
World.content:
A year-long wildlife study at Reserva Conchal in Guanacaste documented 79 species of mammals, birds and reptiles, nearly double the 40 recorded during the property’s previous monitoring period in 2023–2024. The research was carried out at the Conchal Mixed National Wildlife Refuge using 20 camera traps placed at different points across the property.

The cameras operated for a year, recording wildlife activity and providing researchers with a broader look at animal life within Guanacaste’s tropical dry forest. The monitoring identified 28 mammal species, 48 bird species and three reptile species. White-nosed coatis, white-tailed deer, raccoons, opossums and coyotes were among the animals recorded with the greatest relative abundance.

The most notable findings involved Costa Rica’s wild cats. Cameras confirmed the presence of pumas, ocelots, known locally as manigordos, and jaguarundis. The study reported three puma records, 14 ocelots and six jaguarundis, along with evidence of reproduction, including a female ocelot accompanied by a cub.

The presence of large and medium-sized predators is being viewed by Reserva Conchal as an encouraging sign for the refuge, particularly because wild cats depend on functioning habitat and adequate prey populations. “Each species recorded gives us valuable information about the health of the ecosystem,” said Gabriela Meza, Sustainability Manager at Reserva Conchal.

Meza said the monitoring gives conservation teams a stronger scientific basis for deciding where future protection efforts should be concentrated. The increase from 40 species in the previous monitoring period to 79 in the latest survey is substantial, although it should be interpreted as an increase in species detected rather than evidence that wildlife populations themselves nearly doubled.

The publicly available report does not provide enough methodological detail to determine how directly the two monitoring periods can be compared. Reserva Conchal carries out its wildlife work with the Tempisque Conservation Area, McGill University in Canada, the SalveMonos Foundation and the Baulas-Conchal Marine-Coastal Biological Corridor. The partnerships are focused on wildlife research and maintaining connections between habitat areas used by animals moving through this part of Guanacaste.

More than 60 wildlife crossings have also been installed on the property in recent years. The crossings are intended to reduce vehicle strikes and electrocutions, two threats that can become more serious where wildlife habitat overlaps with roads, power infrastructure and tourism development.

Reserva Conchal has also incorporated artificial intelligence into biodiversity analysis, using technology alongside camera-trap monitoring to help researchers process wildlife information and guide conservation decisions. Previous reports on the property’s environmental programs have also documented its use of camera traps, wildlife crossings and collaboration with McGill University and SalveMonos.

The refuge is officially listed by Costa Rica’s National System of Conservation Areas, or SINAC, as the Conchal National Wildlife Refuge under the mixed category. It is located in the Cabo Velas district of Santa Cruz, Guanacaste.

Conservation work at Reserva Conchal also extends to schools in surrounding communities. Since 2017, its Simbiosis environmental education program has reached more than 3,700 students through activities involving biodiversity, ecosystem conservation, pollinators, reforestation and sustainability.

The program brings children and young people into direct contact with the natural environment, rather than limiting environmental education to the classroom. For Reserva Conchal, the latest camera-trap results offer another measure of what wildlife continues to use a landscape that combines protected habitat with one of Guanacaste’s best-known tourism areas.

Continued monitoring will be especially important in determining whether the expanded species list represents a lasting trend and how wild cats and other animals move through the refuge as development continues along Costa Rica’s northern Pacific coast.

World.title: Costa Rica Free-Zone Growth Slows to Weakest Pace Since 2020
World.content:
Growth in Costa Rica’s free-zone economy slowed sharply in June, falling to its weakest pace since 2020 and extending a year-long deceleration in one of the country’s most important economic sectors. Economic activity among companies operating under Costa Rica’s special regimes, which include most free-zone companies, grew 2.9% in June compared with the same month a year earlier, according to the latest Monthly Economic Activity Index, or IMAE, from the Central Bank of Costa Rica.

That was down from 17.2% annual growth in June 2025 and marked the 12th consecutive month in which the sector’s growth rate slowed. The Central Bank attributed much of the slowdown to weaker growth among manufacturers, particularly medical-device producers, as well as lower output of metal products such as electronic components and circuit boards. Professional and administrative services, including advertising, also lost momentum.

Free-zone manufacturing grew just 1.2% year over year in June. Manufacturing outside the special regime performed even worse, contracting 0.9%. The numbers matter because Costa Rica has built much of its recent export and foreign-investment success around free-zone companies, particularly medical-device manufacturers, technology firms and business-service operations.

The latest data do not show that Costa Rica’s free-zone model is collapsing or that companies are leaving the country in large numbers. Much of the slowdown follows an unusually strong period of expansion in 2025. Earlier this year, the Central Bank warned that the pace of growth in the special regime could continue moderating because it was being compared with exceptionally strong results from the previous year.

Still, the speed of the slowdown is notable. Overall economic activity in Costa Rica grew 3% in June, 2.2 percentage points less than in June 2025. Businesses operating outside the special regimes grew 3.1%, meaning the domestic economy slightly outperformed the free-zone sector during the month.

That represents a significant reversal from much of the past several years, when free-zone companies were among the main engines pulling national growth higher. The softer free-zone performance has already affected the broader economic outlook. In April, the Central Bank projected that Costa Rica’s economy would grow 3.5% in 2026, down from an earlier forecast of 3.8%.

At the time, it projected 5.5% growth for the special-regime economy, compared with preliminary growth of 12.7% in 2025. Researchers at the University of Costa Rica were somewhat more cautious in June, forecasting overall economic growth of 3.4% this year and growth of about 4% in the special regime.

They identified slower free-zone activity as one of the main reasons for the weaker national outlook.Not every part of Costa Rica’s economy slowed in June. Construction expanded 9.5%, helped by private projects and a 12.2% increase in public works. The Central Bank pointed to road and bridge projects, emergency reconstruction work and improvements at Juan Santamaría International Airport as contributors to the increase.

Services grew 3.9%, while commerce expanded 2.7%. Hotels and restaurants were among the service activities that grew faster than a year earlier. Agriculture barely grew, at 0.1%, as stronger banana, root-crop, beef and egg production was offset by declines in pineapple and coffee.



For Costa Rica, the question over the coming months will be whether the slowdown in free zones settles at a more normal growth rate after the exceptional gains of 2025 or develops into a broader competitiveness problem. The June numbers alone do not answer that question. They do, however, show that the part of Costa Rica’s economy that has delivered some of its strongest growth in recent years is no longer expanding at anything close to the pace seen a year ago.

World.title: Costa Rica Looks to Ukraine for Drone Technology in Security Fight
World.content:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and Costa Rican President Laura Fernández exchanged invitations for official visits during a phone call yesterday, as the two leaders also discussed possible security cooperation involving Ukraine’s experience with drone technology. Zelensky invited Fernández to visit Ukraine, while the Costa Rican president invited Zelensky to Costa Rica, according to Ukraine’s presidential office and reports on the conversation.



Zelensky used the call to thank Costa Rica for its support for Ukraine in international forums, including votes on United Nations General Assembly resolutions concerning the war with Russia. He also highlighted Costa Rica’s backing for efforts to return Ukrainian children taken to Russia and initiatives aimed at holding Russia accountable for the war.

Ukraine said it had recovered 2,368 children as of early July. For Costa Rica, however, one of the most significant parts of the conversation centered on security. In a video of the call released by the Costa Rican government, Fernández said Costa Rica has a strong interest in learning from Ukraine’s experience with drone-based defense technology.

She linked that interest to her government’s efforts to modernize Costa Rica’s security capabilities as the country confronts drug trafficking and transnational organized crime. Ukraine has become one of the world’s leading developers and users of drone technology during its war with Russia, using unmanned aircraft for surveillance, reconnaissance, communications and battlefield operations.

Zelensky said Costa Rica had expressed specific interest in Ukraine’s security experience. The two presidents agreed that their teams would continue discussions and explore a possible format for a future meeting. No date or location for such a meeting was announced.

The exchange of invitations does not necessarily mean either presidential visit is being actively planned. Invitations between heads of state are common diplomatic gestures, and neither government has announced a timetable, itinerary or formal preparations for a visit. A trip by Fernández to Ukraine would also involve substantial security and logistical considerations because of the ongoing war.

Costa Rica has not indicated that preparations for such a visit are underway. A Zelensky visit to Costa Rica would avoid those complications, but there is similarly no indication that a trip to San José is imminent. For now, the more concrete outcome of yesterday’s conversation appears to be the possibility of technical cooperation on security.

That could move forward through government ministries, security officials and technical teams without requiring either president to travel. For Costa Rica, Ukraine’s rapidly developed expertise with drones could be particularly relevant for surveillance of borders, coastlines and areas used by organized crime and drug trafficking networks.

The conversation also adds a new dimension to relations between Costa Rica and Ukraine. San José has consistently supported Ukraine diplomatically since Russia’s full-scale invasion began in 2022, while the Fernández government is now exploring whether that relationship can produce practical security cooperation at home.

World.title: Latin American Qualifiers Face Double-Duty Day at Cincinnati Open
World.content:
Latin America’s Cincinnati Open contingent faces a high-pressure Wednesday after severe weather disrupted the opening day of qualifying, leaving several players from the region with unfinished business and the possibility of playing twice in one day. Four Latin American players entered Wednesday still in contention for spots in the main draw: Argentina’s Marco Trungelliti and Nadia Podoroska, along with Colombians Nicolás Mejía and Emiliana Arango.

The most intriguing possibility comes on the women’s side. Arango and Podoroska were placed in neighboring sections of the qualifying draw, and both had first-round matches carried into Wednesday. If both advance, they are scheduled to face each other later in the day for a place in the Cincinnati main draw.

Arango, the No. 10 qualifying seed, faces Aliaksandra Sasnovich, while former French Open semifinalist Podoroska takes on No. 16 seed Ella Seidel of Germany. The winners are scheduled to meet no earlier than 4 p.m. Wednesday. That creates a straightforward scenario for Latin American tennis: victories by both would guarantee either Colombia or Argentina another representative when main-draw play begins Thursday.

The men’s qualifying picture offers its own storyline. Trungelliti survived one of Tuesday’s tightest completed matches, rallying past Austria’s Sebastian Ofner 4-6, 6-4, 7-6(4). The 36-year-old Argentine now gets one of the biggest names in qualifying, former world No. 4 Kei Nishikori, with a main-draw place at stake.

Nishikori had his own difficult opening round, defeating Argentina’s Francisco Comesaña 6-4, 1-6, 7-5. Their meeting with Trungelliti gives Argentina another chance to prevent the Japanese veteran from reaching the main draw. Colombia’s Mejía has an even longer potential Wednesday ahead of him.

His first-round match against Britain’s Jacob Fearnley was pushed onto the Wednesday schedule. The winner is then scheduled to return after suitable rest to face either American Marcos Giron or Portugal’s Henrique Rocha for a place in the main draw. The compressed schedule is a direct consequence of Tuesday’s weather.

Severe storms delayed qualifying at the Lindner Family Tennis Center, where 48 men’s and 48 women’s qualifying matches had originally been scheduled across the two-day preliminary event. Twelve qualifiers from each draw will advance into the 96-player main draws. Several Latin American players have already been eliminated. Brazil’s Gustavo Heide fell 6-3, 6-4 to top qualifying seed Luca Van Assche, while Bolivia’s Hugo Dellien lost 6-3, 6-1 to Sho Shimabukuro. Comesaña’s narrow loss to Nishikori also ended his attempt to qualify.

On the women’s side, Mexico’s Renata Zarazúa and Argentina’s Solana Sierra were eliminated in the first qualifying round. Zarazúa, the No. 2 seed, lost to China’s Yue Yuan, while Japan’s Aoi Ito defeated sixth-seeded Sierra. Regardless of Wednesday’s qualifying results, Latin America already has several players waiting in the main draw. Brazil’s João Fonseca and Argentina’s Francisco Cerúndolo are among the men entered directly, while Colombia’s Camila Osorio opens against American Taylor Townsend.

The Osorio-Townsend winner would move on to face No. 2 seed Elena Rybakina. Main-draw play begins Thursday at the Cincinnati Open, one of the final major hard-court events before the U.S. Open.

World.title: Costa Rica Named Among Top Destinations for Solo Travelers
World.content:
Costa Rica has been included among 25 of the world’s best destinations for people traveling alone in a 2026 selection by Travel + Leisure, which highlighted the mix of outdoor adventure, beaches and places where visitors can slow down between activities. The list, published June 11, describes Costa Rica as particularly well suited to adventurous solo travelers.

Among the experiences singled out are whitewater rafting on the Reventazón River, ziplining through rainforest, waterfall rappelling and hiking around Arenal Volcano National Park. Travel + Leisure also points to the hot springs around Arenal as an option for travelers looking for a quieter break and highlights Pacific beaches near Manuel Antonio as popular choices for women traveling alone.

Costa Rica was one of 25 countries selected for the list alongside destinations including Thailand, Albania, Germany, Vietnam, Iceland, Japan and Denmark. The publication did not present the countries as a numbered ranking, meaning Costa Rica was included among the recommended destinations rather than assigned a specific position.

The recognition fits Costa Rica’s long-established tourism pitch: a relatively small country where travelers can move between volcanoes, rainforests and beaches while choosing from activities ranging from wildlife watching and hiking to surfing and rafting.

For solo visitors, that variety can be especially attractive because many of the country’s most popular activities are offered as guided day trips. Destinations such as La Fortuna and Manuel Antonio also have well-developed tourism infrastructure, allowing travelers to arrange excursions without necessarily traveling as part of a larger group.

The international recognition comes during a mixed year for Costa Rica tourism. During the first half of 2026, Costa Rica received 1.73 million international visitors through all entry points, up 7% from the same period in 2025. Air arrivals reached 1.61 million, an increase of 7.8%, according to figures from the Costa Rican Tourism Institute. The United States remained by far the country’s largest source market, sending 966,661 air travelers during the six-month period.

June, however, interrupted the upward trend. Air arrivals fell 1.2% from a year earlier, from 217,120 visitors in June 2025 to 214,518 in June 2026. Tourism officials attributed the decline to several factors, including geopolitical uncertainty, higher aviation fuel prices and travel surrounding the World Cup.

That makes international endorsements particularly useful as Costa Rica competes for travelers in an increasingly crowded tourism market. For people considering visiting alone, Costa Rica offers plenty of advantages, but solo travel still requires the usual precautions. Travelers should pay attention to transportation arrangements, avoid leaving valuables unattended on beaches or in vehicles and use additional caution when moving alone at night, particularly in unfamiliar areas.

Travel + Leisure’s selection ultimately focuses less on traveling alone as an end in itself than on destinations where travelers have enough activities and flexibility to build a trip around their own interests. On that measure, Costa Rica remains firmly in the international conversation.

World.title: Fonseca and Cerúndolo Drawn Into the Same Cincinnati Quarter
World.content:
The 2026 Cincinnati Open draws were released Tuesday, and Latin America’s two most prominent men landed in the same crowded section of the bracket. Brazil’s João Fonseca, seeded 23rd, and Argentina’s Francisco Cerúndolo, seeded 20th, were both placed in the third quarter headed by American Taylor Fritz, a section that also contains 2019 champion Daniil Medvedev, 2021 runner-up Andrey Rublev, Norway’s Casper Ruud, American Brandon Nakashima, Belgian Zizou Bergs and wildcard Marin Čilić, who won the tournament in 2016.

The two cannot meet before the quarterfinals. Both will have to survive a section stacked with former Masters 1000 winners to get there. The draw arrives under unusual circumstances. World Nos. 1 and 2 Jannik Sinner and Carlos Alcaraz, who won the last two men’s titles at the Lindner Family Tennis Center, are both absent, Sinner with a knee injury and Alcaraz with a wrist injury.

Their withdrawals leave the men’s field without the two players who have decided nearly every major hard-court event of the past two seasons. Alexander Zverev, the 2021 champion, acknowledged the shift in an assessment of the field, noting Sinner’s record streak of 34 consecutive Masters 1000 match victories and six titles this year.

“I think it does change things a little bit, especially with Jannik not being here,” Zverev said. “But for me, it doesn’t change much. I still want to compete against the best.” Chile’s Alejandro Tabilo, seeded 22nd, drew a different assignment. He was placed in Zverev’s quarter alongside Flavio Cobolli, the rising Spaniard Rafael Jodar, American Tommy Paul, Valentin Vacherot of Monaco, Belgian Alexander Blockx, Hubert Hurkacz and Denis Shapovalov.

Peru’s Ignacio Buse, seeded 29th at 21 years old, sits in the bottom quarter. That section is headed by second seed Félix Auger-Aliassime and includes Ben Shelton, Lorenzo Musetti, Americans Learner Tien and Frances Tiafoe, France’s Ugo Humbert and Arthur Rinderknech, Stefanos Tsitsipas and 2017 champion Grigor Dimitrov.

Argentina’s Tomás Martín Etcheverry is seeded 26th. All 32 seeds receive a bye into the second round. Argentina again brought the region’s largest delegation, with eight men across the seeded and unseeded ranks. One of them has already made an impression on this swing.

Thiago Agustín Tirante beat Fritz in the Round of 64 in Montreal, an upset that cost the American the tournament he entered as a favorite and that now shadows the quarter Fritz heads in Ohio. On the women’s side, Colombia’s Camila Osorio is the region’s only player in the main draw. She opens against American Taylor Townsend, with the winner advancing to face world No. 2 Elena Rybakina.

It is an unforgiving path for a player who has spent the season rebuilding her ranking, though Townsend is beatable and the reward for an upset would be the highest-profile match of Osorio’s summer. Brazil’s Beatriz Haddad Maia, listed on early entry publications, will not appear.

The former world No. 10 announced last week that she will not play again on tour this year and intends to return in 2027 using a protected ranking, after a season that produced a 4-19 record and eight consecutive losses. Four Latin American women entered qualifying instead. Argentina’s Solana Sierra went out Tuesday evening to Japan’s Aoi Ito, 6-1, 6-1, leaving Colombia’s Emiliana Arango, Argentina’s Nadia Podoroska and Mexico’s Renata Zarazúa to chase the twelve main-draw places on offer.



In the men’s qualifying, 36-year-old Argentine Marco Trungelliti came through his opener against Sebastian Ofner in three sets, while Bolivia’s Hugo Dellien and Colombia’s Nicolás Mejía were still in action late Tuesday. Main-draw play begins Thursday and runs through Aug. 23, the last significant test before the US Open. For a region sending fourteen players to Ohio, the answers about form and readiness will come quickly.

World.title: Galen University unveils Dr. Dorian Allan Barrow STEAAM, AI & Robotics Center
World.content:
Galen University unveils Dr. Dorian Allan Barrow STEAAM, AI & Robotics Center

By Zoila Palma: Today, Galen University proudly unveiled the Dr. Dorian Allan Barrow STEAAM, AI & Robotics Center.

The Dr. Dorian Allan Barrow STEAAM, AI & Robotics Center was launched in honor and recognition of Dr. Barrow’s lasting contributions to higher education and his commitment to the advancement of science, technology, engineering, arts, agriculture, mathematics, artificial intelligence, and robotics.

“This Center represents a commitment to innovation, curiosity, creativity, and possibility. It is a space where students can explore new ideas, develop future-ready skills, and imagine solutions that can shape Belize and the world,” Galen University expressed.

May the Dr. Dorian Allan Barrow STEAAM, AI & Robotics Center continue to inspire generations to learn, create, innovate, and lead.

World.title: United Nations Population Fund Youth camp empowers 97 young Belizeans to become community leaders
World.content:
United Nations Population Fund Youth camp empowers 97 young Belizeans to become community leaders

By Zoila Palma: Ninety-seven young people from Belize, Stann Creek and Toledo districts have strengthened their leadership, advocacy and life skills through the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA) and Department of Youth Services (DYS) “Let’s Be Leaders!” Youth Training Camp.

The four-day residential program was delivered across three weekends, providing participants with practical knowledge and skills aimed at building their confidence and preparing them to take on leadership roles and advocate for positive change in their communities.

Throughout the camp, participants took part in interactive educational sessions, leadership training and cultural activities in a safe and inclusive environment.

The program encouraged young people to build meaningful connections, strengthen their self-confidence and develop the ability to make informed decisions about their lives and futures.

Mackeva Westby-Neal, Acting Liaison Officer for the UNFPA Office in Belize, said the initiative represents an important investment in Belize’s youth. She emphasized that providing young people with knowledge, confidence and agency can help nurture future leaders who can contribute to a more equitable and resilient Belize.

The training camp forms part of the “Let’s Be Clear” campaign under the “Leave No One Behind: Reduction of Adolescent Pregnancy” project, funded by the Grand Duchy of Luxembourg and the Government of Ireland through Irish Aid.

The initiative promotes access to accurate, age-appropriate information on sexual and reproductive health, gender equality and healthy relationships, while encouraging young people to become advocates for their own wellbeing and that of others.

World.title: From Security to Property maintenance: Service businesses Belizeans should consider!
World.content:
From Security to Property maintenance: Service businesses Belizeans should consider!

By Zoila Palma: When we talk about jobs and economic opportunities in Belize, the conversation often focuses on becoming a teacher, nurse, police officer, accountant or obtaining a university degree.

But there is another side of the economy that deserves far more attention: service-based businesses.

From tourism and transportation to security, technology, maintenance and skilled trades, Belize needs people who can provide reliable services to households, businesses and visitors.

The demand is being driven by the growth and changing needs of the economy.

Belize’s 2026 national budget reported that job creation in 2025 was driven by service-oriented industries, particularly wholesale and retail trade and tourism.

Tourism remains one of the country’s major economic engines, supporting tens of thousands of jobs directly and indirectly. The World Bank has also identified skilled-labour shortages in Belize and says its new country strategy will focus on developing a better-skilled workforce.

So, what types of service businesses could Belize use more of?

Tourism and Experience Services

Examples: tour companies, tour guides, transportation services, eco-tourism operators, cultural tours, fishing and adventure excursions, event planners and destination-management companies.

Tourism creates opportunities far beyond hotels and restaurants. The World Bank’s current Belize strategy identifies tourism as an important area for investment and job creation.

Security Services

Examples: private security companies, security guards, CCTV installation and monitoring, alarm systems, access-control systems and security consulting.

As businesses, homes, construction sites and commercial properties expand, there is an opportunity for professional security companies offering more than traditional guards. Belize is also investing heavily in security infrastructure, including communications systems and an AI-enabled systems, creating opportunities for people trained in security technology.

Cleaning and Property-Maintenance Services

Examples: residential cleaning, commercial cleaning, post-construction cleaning, landscaping, lawn care, pressure washing, pool maintenance and property caretaking.

This is an area where relatively small businesses can start with limited equipment and grow. Hotels, offices, rental properties, restaurants, schools and homeowners all require regular maintenance.

Construction and Home-Improvement Services

Examples: electrical work, plumbing, carpentry, welding, masonry, painting, roofing, cabinetry, tiling, air-conditioning installation and general maintenance.

These are exactly the kinds of practical skills that can become businesses. A trained electrician, plumber, carpenter or welder does not necessarily need to wait for someone to hire them—they can build a customer base and eventually employ other Belizeans.

Information Technology and Digital Services

Examples: computer repair, website development, cybersecurity, cloud services, data analysis, digital marketing, graphic design and IT support.

The Government of Belize has identified cybersecurity, data analysis, UI/UX design and cloud engineering as among the most in-demand and currently lacking skills in the country’s global digital services sector.

Transportation and Delivery Services

Examples: airport transfers, tourist transportation, courier services, delivery companies, moving services, refrigerated transportation and specialized freight services.

As tourism, e-commerce, construction and business activity grow, so does the need to move people and products efficiently. Transportation is also closely connected to tourism and other sectors, meaning a well-run transportation company can serve multiple markets.

Agricultural and Agro-Processing Services

Examples: farm services, irrigation installation, agricultural equipment repair, food processing, packaging, cold storage, transportation and agricultural consulting.

Agriculture is not only about farming. There are businesses to be created around the farmer—from planting and harvesting services to processing, packaging, storage and transportation.

But for Belizeans to take advantage of these opportunities, we must also invest in the skills needed to provide these services.

Belize therefore needs to promote technical and vocational education, apprenticeships and entrepreneurship at the same time.

Schools can expose students to trades and practical skills earlier, businesses can provide more apprenticeship opportunities, and training institutions can work closely with employers to identify the skills the economy actually needs.

The goal should not only be to prepare young Belizeans to look for jobs, but also to equip them with the skills to create businesses, provide needed services and, eventually, employ others.

World.title: The skills Belize needs most: Why we need to promote Vo-Tech
World.content:
The skills Belize needs most: Why we need to promote Vo-Tech

By Zoila Palma: There is a growing conversation in Belize about education, employment and the skills young people need to build successful careers.

While university degrees remain important for many professions, there is also a constant need for people with practical, technical and vocational skills.

The World Bank noted that shortages of skilled labour are evident in Belize and identified workforce skills development as a priority for the country’s economic growth.

Among the skills that deserve greater attention are construction and carpentry, electrical installation, plumbing, automotive and heavy-duty mechanics, welding and metal fabrication, refrigeration and air-conditioning, nursing and healthcare support, information technology and computer repair, hospitality and culinary skills, and agriculture and agro-processing.

These are not simply jobs that can be done while waiting for a “better” career.

They are essential services that homes, businesses, hotels, farms, factories and communities depend on every day.

Our TVET system already provides training pathways in trades at different levels, including programs designed to prepare students for entry-level and skilled work.

The need for these skills also creates opportunities for entrepreneurship.

A trained electrician can start an electrical business.

A welder can open a fabrication shop.

A mechanic can establish an auto-repair service.

A carpenter can build furniture, cabinets and homes.

A trained refrigeration technician can provide services to households, supermarkets, restaurants and hotels.

With the right training, tools, work ethic and business skills, a vocational qualification can become more than a job—it can become a source of income and employment for others.

This is why Belize needs to promote technical and vocational education and training, or TVET, much more aggressively.

For too long, young people have sometimes been given the impression that success means going to university and earning a traditional degree, while vocational careers are treated as a second option.

That mindset needs to change.

An ILO analysis published earlier this year specifically examined Belize’s TVET system and emphasized the importance of developing, recognizing and certifying skills while improving access to training and the labour market.

The question should not be whether a young person chooses university or vocational training.

The better question is: What skills does Belize need, and how can we prepare our young people to fill those gaps?

We need schools, parents, policymakers and businesses to expose students earlier to trades and technical careers, expand apprenticeships and hands-on training, and make vocational education something students can be proud of.

Belize does not only need more people with certificates and degrees—it needs people who can build, repair, install, create, care, cook, design, troubleshoot and produce.

If there is always a need for these skills, there should always be a strong effort to train Belizeans to fill thsse jobs.

World.title: International News: Solar Eclipse plunges parts of Europe into darkness in spectacular display
World.content:
International News: Solar Eclipse plunges parts of Europe into darkness in spectacular display

By Zoila Palma: Millions of people gathered across parts of Europe today to witness a rare total solar eclipse, with stunning images capturing the moment the Moon moved directly between the Earth and the Sun. Large crowds equipped with lawn chairs, umbrellas and hats gathered across northern and central Spain, while parts of Iceland and Greenland also had opportunities to observe the celestial event.

In Iceland, daylight briefly turned into darkness along the western coastline as the eclipse reached totality. Despite concerns about cloudy weather, skies cleared in some areas, allowing residents and tourists to witness the rare phenomenon. In Reykjavik, crowds reportedly cheered as the sky suddenly went dark near the iconic Hallgrímskirkja church. Totality was expected to last less than two and a half minutes, with the eclipse reaching its peak over the waters west of Iceland.

Spain was expected to attract as many as 6 million visitors to rural areas along the eclipse’s path and the Balearic Islands. Officials urged spectators to avoid areas affected by an ongoing heatwave because of increased wildfire risks. The event was particularly significant for Spain, where a total solar eclipse had not been visible across the Iberian Peninsula since 1912.

A total solar eclipse occurs when the Moon completely blocks the Sun’s light, temporarily darkening the day and creating dramatic changes in the sky and surrounding environment. Scientists are also using the event as an opportunity for research, with NASA planning to operate a high-altitude aircraft from Iceland to track the Moon’s shadow while balloon missions study changes in the lower atmosphere. Spain is scheduled to experience another total solar eclipse on August 2, 2027, followed by an annular eclipse in January 2028.
