World.title: Lasha Bugadze becomes first modern Georgian writer whose book was barred from being sent to prison
World.content:
Precedent for literary censorship in Georgia

The administration of Rustavi Prison refused to allow Lasha Bugadze’s new novel, The Observer, to be delivered to the prison. The book was intended for Nana Sander, who was convicted over her participation in a protest on 4 October 2025.

Notably, the penitentiary code contains no provision explicitly banning fiction from being brought into prisons.

The book’s synopsis describes a fictional political reality involving the long rule of a “despot”, the “division of the country into zones” and a “cult of the leader”. It also mentions the scheduling of elections and a decision by the country’s population on whether they should take place.

According to Bugadze, a prison official refused to allow the book in, saying the novel contained “political content”.

The writer says it is unclear to him who determined that the book contained political content and what criteria they used. He suspects the decision may have been prompted by words and phrases in the novel, such as “despot” and “cult of the leader”.

“The employee told me directly that the book could not be delivered because it was political in nature. I don’t think he sat down and read the book. I doubt he even read the synopsis,” Bugadze said.

In his view, someone appears to have judged the work to be political without giving any clear reason.

“Who put this label on the text? [Who decided] whether it was political or not? What does that even mean? And, excuse me, even if the content is political, why should a citizen – whether a prisoner or anyone else – not have the right to read such a book?” the writer said.

Bugadze sees the incident as a potential precedent for censoring literary works:

“It can be described as the first significant example of literary censorship in modern Georgian history. This is an extremely dangerous precedent, and under no circumstances should it be considered normal. The situation requires a response. No one has the right to stop someone from reading.”

The head of the human rights organisation Sapari, Baia Pataraia, announced that legal proceedings would begin over the incident:

“We are taking legal steps. <…> First, we will demand a written and reasoned refusal.”

The organisation PEN Georgia also responded to the case. It described the incident as an alarming precedent for censorship of a literary work, linked not only to the novel’s content but also to the author’s political and civic stance. The organisation stressed that censoring fiction and restricting freedom of expression are unacceptable in a democratic society.

Lasha Bugadze’s The Observer

Precedent for literary censorship in Georgia

World.title: Armenia seeks alternatives amid concerns over possible Russian gas price hike
World.content:
Russian gas pressure on Armenia

If the issue of raising gas tariffs arises, the Armenian authorities will discuss it with their Russian counterparts in a friendly atmosphere, Sargis Khandanyan, an MP from the ruling Civil Contract faction, told journalists.

Khandanyan added that he had no information about any negotiations with Russia over gas tariffs. However, he expressed confidence that, if necessary, Armenia would be able to find alternatives to Russian gas. These could include supplies from Iran, although this is not the only option.

Yerevan and Tehran have already discussed the issue. Following talks held with Iranian partners by Armenia’s Minister of Territorial Administration and Infrastructure, Davit Khudatyan, it emerged that the volume of Iranian gas supplies could potentially be doubled.

“This decision has nothing to do with any other country, Russia in particular. It is a profitable economic activity that both countries are interested in expanding,” the Armenian minister said.

Political analyst Robert Ghevondyan notes that there has recently been increasingly frequent talk of a possible revision of Russian gas prices. He views the issue in the context of the levers of pressure being used against Armenia. In his view, Moscow has already exhausted much of its arsenal and is now resorting to economic leverage, including in the energy sector.

“Political, cultural and terrorist levers, as well as the influence of the criminal subculture, are no longer working for various reasons. And Russia, in order to prevent Armenia from strengthening its independence, has decided to make full use of its last remaining lever,” Ghevondyan said.

‘This scenario cannot be ruled out’: On gas imports from Azerbaijan

Journalists asked MP Sargis Khandanyan how likely it was that the tariff on gas imports from Russia could change by the end of the year.

“I am not aware of when this issue was last discussed with Russia. Nor am I aware of any information that would give grounds to believe that the gas tariff could change,” he replied.

At the same time, the MP noted that the government attaches great importance to diversifying supplies. He recalled the agreements reached during the visit of Armenia’s Minister of Territorial Administration and Infrastructure to Iran. According to him, the “Trump Route” could also be considered as one such opportunity:

“As part of the transit route that will connect Azerbaijan with Nakhchivan through Armenian territory, a gas pipeline will be built. This could provide another opportunity. We could consider this pipeline as an additional source. Of course, this is a very theoretical idea, but it would not be difficult to implement.”

Asked about the possibility of importing gas from Azerbaijan, Khandanyan said that Yerevan and Baku were discussing a broad range of issues:

“I do not know how far we have progressed on the issue of gas supplies, but this scenario cannot be ruled out.”

In late October 2025, Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev announced that all restrictions on transit to Armenia would be lifted. Since then, Armenia has been receiving petroleum products from the neighbouring country by rail. According to official figures, Azerbaijan has already supplied Armenia with 20,000 tonnes of petroleum products.

Yerevan and Tehran agree to increase gas supplies. Can Moscow stand in the way?

Minister of Territorial Administration and Infrastructure Davit Khudatyan paid a three-day visit to Iran. Upon returning from Tehran, he said that the volume of Iranian gas supplied under the “Gas for Electricity” programme could be at least doubled. He explained that the pipeline’s capacity exceeds the volume of gas currently being supplied.

Under the programme, Armenia has been receiving gas from Iran since 2009, converting it into electricity which is then supplied back to Iran.

To increase gas imports and export a corresponding volume of electricity to Iran, construction of the Iran-Armenia high-voltage power transmission line needs to be completed. The Armenian government hopes that the long-delayed project will be completed by the end of the year.

Meanwhile, since 2015, the Armenian section of the pipeline carrying gas from Iran has been controlled by Russian company Gazprom.

As a result, some experts doubt whether Iranian gas supplies can be increased without Moscow’s consent. The Armenian government, however, has assured that there will be no obstacles to expanding supplies under the “Gas for Electricity” programme.

Expert commentaty

Political commentator Artem Yerkanyan says:

“Russian Security Council Deputy Secretary Alexei Shevtsov threatened that unless Armenia revises its foreign policy course, it will have to pay $800 for Russian gas instead of the current $177. Compensating for that difference would cost at least $1bn. That is more than the €50m the European Union has promised Armenia as compensation for the impact of strained relations with Russia.

It is worth explaining what the figures of $177 and $800 actually mean. Russia’s Gazprom sells gas for $177 to Gazprom Armenia, which is owned by Gazprom itself. In other words, it also earns revenue from the distribution of the gas, and that revenue also goes to Gazprom. Therefore, I think it would be incorrect to say that Armenia buys gas for $177.

It is also unclear where the figure of $800 comes from, considering the following:

China buys Russian gas for $258;

Turkey for $280;

Hungary, Serbia and Slovakia for $400;

Spain, France and Belgium for $450.

Moreover, according to a forecast by Russia’s Ministry of Economic Development, by the end of this year the average price at which Russia will sell gas to countries outside the EAEU [an economic bloc led by Russia] will be $290.

If the average price is $290, why are they planning to sell it to Armenia for $800? That is unclear.”

Political analyst Robert Ghevondyan argues:

“Following the elections, the Armenian authorities have continued to pursue a multi-vector foreign policy. Dependence on Russia is steadily declining, with the economic dimension playing an increasingly important role in this process.

While Russia is trying to exert economic pressure, Armenia is opening up new markets that Armenian businesses previously ‘failed to notice’ because of their excessive focus on the Russian market. Although problems remain with some goods, economic diversification is advancing rapidly.

In the energy sector, Armenia has alternatives when it comes to building a new nuclear reactor, which in itself is a headache for Russia.

It is no coincidence that, alongside economic blackmail, Rosatom executives periodically make Armenia ‘attractive’ offers to build a new Russian nuclear reactor. However, the Armenian authorities are likely to opt for a different proposal.

A rise in gas prices could initially cause problems. But Armenia has alternatives here as well: Iranian, Turkmen and now Azerbaijani gas.

Consequently, in the near future, Russian gas may find itself merely competing on the market. This would limit the Kremlin’s ability to use gas prices to blackmail Armenia.

In conclusion, it should be noted that increased pressure from Russia is having the opposite effect. Armenia is steadily ‘freeing itself’ from excessive Russian influence and diversifying its economy. The Kremlin does not appear to recognise this yet, but that is its problem.”

World.title: Kobakhidze: Georgia does not publicly declare Russia an enemy because this would require follow-up steps
World.content:
Georgian prime minister on Russia

Georgian Dream Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze told journalists that the Georgian government does not publicly call Russia an “enemy” because such a political statement would require corresponding action.

A journalist asked Kobakhidze whether the Georgian government considers Russia an enemy. The prime minister replied:

“Your questions are shameful, you look ridiculous. Let me explain in simple terms why this question is shameful: you want to get a sensational headline, even in the Russian media, saying that I have declared the Russian Federation an enemy. This is a specific political statement that would have to be followed by specific steps – roughly the same, or exactly the same, as those your party” (referring to the United National Movement – JAMnews) “took in 2008 and before.”

The journalist asked whether this was precisely why the government was reluctant to openly call Russia an enemy.

“Of course. What, should I repeat it again?!” Kobakhidze replied.

Kobakhidze also addressed Russia’s occupation of Georgian territories and reiterated that the Russian Federation occupies 20% of Georgia’s territory.

“Of course, the Russian Federation is the only state and party that has occupied Georgian territories. This is an absolutely clear fact. Numerous statements have been made about this, and there is no doubt about it,” Kobakhidze stressed.

He said Russia’s occupation of Georgian territory was a “crime against the Georgian state and the Georgian people”:

“This is an egregious crime: first the occupation, and then the so-called recognition.”

World.title: Breaking: Tasmania confirms first case of deadly bird flu strain H5N1
World.content:
Tasmania has confirmed its first case of the deadly H5N1 bird flu that has impacted wildlife across five other Australian states.

Following testing which was completed overnight, a brown skua was confirmed to have had the virus.

The single bird was found at Burgess Cove at Rocky Cape, on the north-west coast of Tasmania.

The Department of Natural Resources and Environment Tasmania (NRE) said it was alerted to the carcass of the bird by staff from the Parks and Wildlife Service, who have been undertaking active surveillance of coastal areas.

Department secretary Jason Jacobi said it was "inevitable" that the virus would arrive in the state.

He said infected brown skuas had been found in other Australian states.

"It's not unexpected that we would find a confirmed brown skua," Mr Jacobi said.

The first detected case of H5 bird flu in Australia, found in WA, was also a brown skua. (iNaturalist: Simon Plat, Brown skua, CC BY-NC 4.0)

Minister for Primary Industries and Water Gavin Pearce said Tasmania was "prepared to respond" and would enact its bird flu response plan.

"We've worked with the commercial poultry sector to assist them in development of biosecurity preparedness plans and ensuring that they are ready to activate those plans," Mr Pearce said.

Brown skuas are large predatory seabirds native to Tasmania that breed on Antarctic and sub-Antarctic islands.

World.title: Is having a romantic AI companion cheating? Some people think so
World.content:
What do you look for in a partner? Emotional support? Good listening skills? Romantic connection?

People are increasingly finding these traits in AI companions and turning to them even when in a committed — human — relationship.

But with romantic and even sexual intimacy possible between a user and AI, is it cheating?

"New studies show about half of people who are in a relationship with an AI companion are also in regular relationship, so it's not just a substitute, but also a complement," says Raffaele Ciriello, an expert in AI companions and digital relationships at the University of Sydney.

He says as an emerging type of relationship, it's up for debate if having an AI companion constitutes as cheating, "just like people debate if ethical non-monogamy can exist".

As the technology continues to evolve, sexologist and couples therapist Isiah McKimmie says people will be forced to continually ask themselves, is this OK for me and my relationship, or does this feel like a breach?

What makes AI companions appealing?

AI companions such as Replika and Character.AI are software programs that use conversation to mimic human-like relationships.

Researchers say creators of AI companion apps often market their chatbots in ways that humanise them, emphasising that qualities they present are "better" than those of human partners.

They offer constant availability and support, and "do not get tired or annoyed", the research reveals.

Dr Ciriello says it's that accessibility, and their ability to be personalised to a user's desires, that makes them so powerful.

"It's this adaptability and customisation that allows the user to feel understood and that they can get more tailored advice from AI than other technology, or even people."

Dr Ciriello says people use them for emotional and sexual purposes, which can feel "exciting and new".

"Novelty is doing a lot of the work … a lot of people are experimenting with this and because sexuality is such an important part of human life, of course people are using AI to explore it."

Ms McKimmie says AI companions are "fantastically appealing" because they are there any time you need them, "and don't come with their own needs".

"Sometimes real humans are too tired or stressed to be able to listen well, or just haven't learnt those skills, or have something going on for them they want to talk through, too.

"[AI] is all of the emotional support that we want, without having to give back."

What the data says

Relationship experts say what crosses the line in one relationship, might not in another. (Pexels: cottonbro studio)

Research from Canada found half of 1,815 people surveyed would consider a partner's romantic AI companion use as infidelity.

The authors said reactions to romantic companions were about as negative as reactions to dating apps and webcamming — both of which involve a human third party.

"They were more negative than reactions to all other sexual technologies, such as AI pornography and sex toys."

The research also found nearly two-thirds of AI romantic companion users kept it a secret.

Australia doesn't have similar data, but a YouGov study revealed one in seven Australians could imagine falling in love with an AI tool.

That rose to 28 per cent among gen Z respondents.

Ms McKimmie says what crosses the line in one relationship might not in another.

"I've worked with couples who came to me for what they call infidelity, for example one partner watching porn.

"For other couples that might be seen as normal, or expected, and even healthy."

Using AI chatbots for relationship advice While the accessibility and "judgement-free zone" of AI chatbots can be attractive when seeking relationship advice, experts warn there are risks you need to be aware of.

Pornography use is just one example. But Dr Ciriello says what sets AI companionship apart from other ethical issues with technology in relationships is sensitive relational disclosure.

"On a porn website you don't typically provide a lot of personal information about yourself, but with an AI companion, that is the whole point."

And some people will consider that a breach of trust or betrayal, he says.

"The fact people are talking about their relationship with AI means people are implicated that haven't necessarily consented to being part of that conversation.

"Sharing sensitive information about other people creates an ethical grey area that is not sufficiently addressed through existing privacy laws and regulations."

Have you found yourself forming a human-like relationship with AI? We'd love to hear from you

How to navigate AI companions in your relationship

Ms McKimmie says it's going to be up to each couple to work out expectations around AI use and come to an agreement on what's appropriate for the relationship.

"Really, it does require talking about it and working through it together as a team.

" We still need this very human ability to communicate when it comes to these issues. "

For those feeling hurt or insecure by their partner's AI companion use, Ms McKimmie suggests approaching the conversation with openness and curiosity, while also sharing your vulnerabilities around it.

"They understandably might be feeling lonely and not good enough … [and] like the relationship is unstable and insecure, and that is really scary."

Engaging a therapist can help navigate these conversations if you aren't making headway alone.

"Professional support can reveal underlying reasons why someone is turning to AI," Ms McKimmie says.

Depending on what your partner is using an AI companion for, Dr Ciriello says consent may also form part of that conversation.

"Relational consent is the biggest concern and probably the most legitimate objection people might have to these relationships."

World.title: Warning for mariners as ghost rig lights goes out
World.content:
An abandoned oil drilling rig rusting away at sea is now raising safety concerns now the platform's lights are no longer working.

The Cliff Head oil platform has been at the centre of a storm over who foots the $200 million clean up bill after junior oil and gas companies Pilot and Triangle energy entered voluntary administration.

Pilot was working with Triangle to repurpose the rig but in July both companies went bust.

Now sitting idle at sea 11 kilometres off the coast of Dongara, about 350 kilometres north of Perth, the rig which has been used as a navigation aid for over a decade remains unlit.

'Extremely dangerous'

The stretch of water where the old drilling rig sits is frequented by mariners including commercial fishermen.

Western Australia's Department of Transport and Major Infrastructure released an alert about the lack of lighting on the oil rig.

Marine Safety WA has advised all mariners in Dongara and Leeman waters to be aware of the 500 metre exclusion zone surrounding the site and to check navigation warnings.

Thomas Mayo says the unlit platform is very dangerous. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

Maritime Union of Australia's assistant national secretary Thomas Mayo said unlit infrastructure out at sea can be a "huge risk for mariners" at night.

"It's very dark out there, you don't have street lights or anything like that [in the ocean]," he said.

"You've got all sorts of weather and conditions to contend with so it's extremely dangerous to have a facility out there unlit.

"These things should be cleaned up quickly after they've finished their time of production."

The Cliff Head platform sits abandoned offshore following the recent voluntary administration of operators Triangle Operations and Pilot Energy. (ABC Midwest and Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

Calls for action

Since the future of the platform has been in doubt, the decommissioning process, including who will pay for it has not been made clear.

Federal resources minister Madeline King previously said "under no circumstances" would the taxpayer be responsible for footing the bill.

"In the event of companies being unable to pay I will have no hesitation in extending the Northern Endeavor levy or taking other measures to cover all costs of decommissioning," she said.

The Cliff Head platform has operated since 2006, but today it sits abandoned off the Dongara coastline. (ABC Midwest and Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

But Mr Mayo said there needed to be "greater action".

"It's an indication of what we would possibly see more of because oil and gas companies are increasingly abandoning platforms like this and not following up with their obligations to do the clean-up after," he said.

"They certainly shouldn't be getting away [without decommissioning] and then putting mariners at danger."

A spokesperson for the administrators said they were aware of concerns regarding the rig's lighting.

Meanwhile a spokesperson for the National Offshore Petroleum Safety and Environmental Management Authority said they were working to reduce hazards "imminently".

"NOPSEMA is aware the facility is currently unlit and is coordinating the deployment of navigational aids which includes lighting," they said.

"In the interim, information about the facility's location and status is available to mariners through navigational safety information issued by maritime authorities."

World.title: How a 1mm error had Supercars champ driving a slower car all season
World.content:
Supercars and Triple Eight Race Engineering have both responded after the revelation that 2024 champion Will Brown has been driving with an engine airflow restrictor that is 1 millimetre undersized all season.

Throughout 25 races in 2026, Brown has achieved one pole position and two podiums, while teammate Broc Feeney has five wins in what should be similar machinery.

But on Tuesday night, following a poor outing for Brown in Perth two weekends ago, Red Bull Triple Eight Race Engineering found Brown's Ford Mustang has been underpowered all season.

"After Perth we promised Will, his crew and all stakeholders associated with Car #888, which includes our beloved fans, that we would leave no stone unturned and find reasons why Car #888 has not been fighting for race wins recently," team principal Jamie Whincup said.

"At 7pm [Tuesday] night we found a significant issue on Car #888.

"Since the start of this season, Car #888 has been running with an undersized engine airflow restrictor. This part manages the airflow into the engine and has a significant negative impact on engine performance, and therefore lap time.

"This is not a part we, Triple Eight or Red Bull Ampol Racing, manufacture. This is a supplied part from Supercars expected to be the same for all 11 Ford Mustangs, distributed at the start of the season and expected to be run for the whole season."

Will Brown has just two podiums from 25 races this season. (Getty Images: Daniel Kalisz)

Whincup said the undersized part was costing Brown 0.15 seconds per lap, explaining why the Red Bull Triple Eight Race Engineering driver has struggled for pace often this year.

"We as a team are taking responsibility and want to deeply apologise to everyone involved for allowing this to happen," Whincup said.

"While this error has cost our team a considerable amount of resource, sport is an emotional game and these types of things have knock-on effects bigger than the average 1.5 tenths a lap.

"We will be taking up with Supercars why they have supplied us with what is a controlled component out of specification, which has negatively impacted the performance of Car #888 this season to date.

"We will continue to roll out our new chassis for Car #888 at Queensland Raceway and look forward to measuring our capability now we are competing with the same horsepower as the rest of the field."

On Wednesday, Supercars acknowledged the revelation that Will Brown's car had been fitted with an air restrictor, provided by them, that was 1mm too small.

However, Supercars said the undersized restrictor was only supposed to be used for demonstration purposes only, provided for the team to do a launch in Geelong in February.

"The component was loaned by Supercars to Triple Eight Race Engineering (T8RE) for demonstration purposes only at the team's launch in February.

"The air restrictor subsequently remained fitted to Car 888 through the Perth Super 440. Neither party identified the discrepancy until it was discovered by T8RE during preparations for next weekend's event in Ipswich.

"Throughout the Supercars season, routine scrutineering and compliance checks are carried out at random by Supercars' technical department, covering a vast range of components and systems. As of the Perth event, the air restrictor fitted to Car 888 had not been selected for inspection during those checks.

"Supercars is reviewing the circumstances surrounding this matter and will evaluate opportunities to strengthen its technical and operational procedures moving forward.

"Supercars acknowledges and appreciates T8RE's identifying and prompt reporting of the matter to Supercars."

Brown will now be driving with an engine on parity with the other Mustangs during the next round at Queensland Raceway in Ipswich on August 21-23.

World.title: Remote school bus axed leaving students and families stranded
World.content:
Hailed as a remote success story, Queensland's longest school bus service has been axed, leaving six primary students stranded from their school.

For the last six years up to 18 students in the remote towns of Bidunggu and Gregory, about 300 kilometres north of Mount Isa, have made the three-hour daily return trip to Burketown State School to learn alongside peers in the classroom.

But during the last school holidays, Bidunggu resident and parent Natalie King said families were told the bus service would not resume in term three, leaving boarding school or School of the Air as the only educational options.

The next nearest primary school from Gregory is 165km away at Doomadgee, but there is no school bus.

"This bus gave them a chance to be with teachers in person … for students to have that kind of normal school experience," Ms King said.

"These kids need an education."

The wheels are coming off

The bus service was established in 2021 after Burketown State School approached the community to create a regular bus service and boost enrolments, which, according to the Department of Education, currently sit around 27 students.

Ms King said the 240km round trip each day was not ideal but resulted in far better outcomes than remote schooling.

"I sent my young fellow away to boarding school in Cairns after he graduated from Burketown. The teachers down there couldn't believe how well educated he was," she said.

"That's the sort of education we were getting."

The lengthy bus ride is 120km long, or roughly 90 minutes. (ABC North West Qld: Emily Dobson)

The service was funded by the Department of Transport and Main Roads (TMR) and was operated by Burketown State School until last term.

Burketown State School declined to comment.

A Queensland Department of Education spokesperson said the state school had worked hard to try and find a replacement operator.

"The Department of Education is working closely with the principal to identify any eligible drivers within the school community; however, the very limited availability of suitably qualified drivers and staff absences have impacted the continuity of the bus service," the spokesperson said.

"The Mount Isa School of the Air is liaising with the three families and six students to engage in further education.

"We will continue to liaise with TMR, who are investigating if there are any options for the bus to be run by the council or other community-based groups."

A TMR spokesperson confirmed funding was available for the service, but no replacement had been found so far.

Calls for a school

Monique Mckerrell's family fell in love with the area on a cross-country road trip. (Supplied: Monique Mckerrell)

Gregory resident Monique Mckerrell moved to the region with her two children after being amazed by the area's natural beauty.

"We were planning on travelling Australia … we found Gregory and fell in love," she said.

"The spring that runs all year round to swim in, fish in, there's lots of hunting that we enjoy doing too, it was just prime."

Monique Mckerrell fears that as her children get older they will miss out on the same schooling and social experience other kids receive. (Supplied: Monique Mckerrell)

But the bus service's closure has raised questions about what future is possible in a town without access to face-to-face schooling.

"Going to school is an important life experience, learning how to be part of the world, communicating, listening, thinking, and trying new things, and then gaining that confidence away from home," she said.

"If you had a school [in Gregory], it would bring more people in the community … in the long run I would prefer a physical school in town."

Gregory previously had a primary school — a campus of Doomadgee State School — between 2003 and 2012, which closed after enrolments dwindled to four students.

But the community has grown.

According to the most recent census data, Gregory has a population of 122 people, about 60 per cent more than the 2016 census.

Meanwhile, Burketown, where the region's only school remains, recorded a population of 204 people in 2021, down 34 residents from 2016

Ms King agreed a school at Gregory was needed as raising children without access to face-to-face learning was "too hard".

"It's just so sad because a lot of families, they want to come home, they want to come back … but now that we've got no school it's too hard."

A Department of Education spokesperson said little evidence supported the construction of a new school in the Gregory area.

Natalie King said the school bus service gave students a chance to play, socialise and learn face-to-face. (ABC North West Qld: Emily Dobson)

"When planning for new schools, the department considers a broad range of factors to establish a service need to provide a new school," the spokesperson said.

"For most new schools in Queensland, the service need is underpinned by an analysis of the local school network and its ability to meet projected population growth."

World.title: P-plater who ploughed car into herd of cattle recounts 'terrifying' ordeal
World.content:
A P-plate driver who ploughed through a herd of cows at 110 kilometres an hour on a country highway in the dark, killing several, has described his "terrifying" experience.

WARNING: This story contains descriptions and photographs of dying animals that may be distressing.

Police say Hervic Declarador, 19, was lucky to escape with his life after the "intense and harrowing" incident.

The accident happened about 10pm on Sunday as Mr Declarador was driving his brand-new ute on South Coast Highway near Marbelup, about 420km south of Perth.

He had bought the car just two weeks earlier.

Mr Declarador said he had little time to brake before hitting the herd. (Supplied: Hervic Declarador)

"I was just driving normally and then everything exploded in my face ... I had ringing in my ears, and everything went black, and there were airbags all over me," he said.

" It was terrifying, it just happened too fast. "

Hidden danger

The accident happened on an unlit stretch of the highway connecting the city of Albany to the tourist town of Denmark on WA's south coast.

Mr Declarador said he had been blinded by the lights of a car parked on the side of the road as he rounded a corner.

The car's driver had apparently been trying to alert other motorists to the cows, but Mr Declarador said the high beam had instead obscured the danger ahead.

Several cows were killed or injured in the crash. (Supplied: Hervic Declarador)

"I was thinking 'oh, what a dickhead' and as I got closer, I tried to flash them to try and turn them off, but when I flashed my own high beams, that's when I saw the cows," he said.

" I was only 15 metres away from the cows, give or take, and I didn't have time to brake ... I just smashed right into them. "

Car 'unrecognisable'

The 19-year-old said he initially thought the damage was relatively minor because of the car's safety features, but that relief was short-lived.

"I didn't really feel the impact because the airbags just caught me so well that I thought it was just going to be a big dent," he said.

The brand new car was unrecognisable after the crash. (Supplied: Hervic Declarador)

But once outside, he saw the full extent of the carnage.

"There was a cow on the ground, still alive, couldn't move, looking at me with tears in its eyes," he said.

"And then I saw my car … the whole bonnet was caved in, dented in and just unrecognisable."

Fallen tree freed cows

Great Southern Police Superintendent John Munday said about 50 cows had wandered onto the road after a tree felled by strong winds landed on a fence.

Officers who attended found four dead cows on the road and euthanised a further three injured cows at the scene.

Mr Declarador had purchased the vehicle two weeks earlier. (Supplied: Hervic Declarador)

He said police had not spoken to the driver who tried to warn Mr Declarador of the cows, but believed they were acting in the interests of other drivers.

"I think they were probably trying to do the best thing they could at the time, but equally, I can put myself in the shoes of that driver to be really unsure as to what's going on," he said.

Mr Declarador said he had been blinded by the high beams of a parked vehicle. (Supplied: Hervic Declarador)

He described the incident as "intense and harrowing", with Mr Declarador lucky to walk away without serious injury,

"These incidents, they're extremely dangerous, and there have been multiple occurrences where there are fatalities and serious injuries where cars have hit any sort of livestock, native animal on the road," he said.

" It's just fortunate nobody was hurt, and the car stayed on its wheels. "

Superintendent Munday said no charges had been laid, and responsibility for the investigation had been handed to the City of Albany.

There have been several recent reports of livestock wandering onto public roads across the Great Southern, with some residents saying it was only a matter of time until they caused a serious incident.

A livestock warning remains in place for the stretch of highway where the accident happened, with motorists advised to exercise extreme caution.

World.title: Aussie man charged with fraud, child indecency in US
World.content:
A convicted fraudster notorious for his dating app antics in regional New South Wales has been hit with fresh charges on the other side of the world.

Brett Joseph, 39, made claims of immense wealth to a woman he met on dating apps, when in reality he had a humble upbringing in Mudgee, in the state's Central West.

He was eventually convicted of several counts of fraud in Mudgee Local Court in 2016, before moving to Texas in the United States — where he is again alleged to have fallen on the wrong side of the law.

Do you know more about this or have a similar story? Email turner-cohen.alex@abc.net.au

Brett Joseph made the rounds on dating apps across regional NSW. (Supplied: Daisy Armstrong)

Texas police charged Mr Joseph with the fraudulent use or possession of identifying information last Wednesday.

He has not yet been indicted, the Wharton District Court confirmed.

Arresting officers from the Throckmorton Sheriff's Department told the ABC they served Mr Joseph with papers relating to a civil case, but after running his drivers licence discovered there was an outstanding arrest warrant for fraud.

A mugshot taken in October last year, when Joseph was charged with child indecency. (Supplied: Throckmorton County Sheriff's Office)

"We confirmed the warrant and placed him under arrest and transported [him] to the Stephens County Jail," Sheriff Glen Whitfield said.

A booking sheet and accompanying mugshot shows Mr Joseph spent two days behind bars before posting a $US10,000 ($14,200) bond.

Decade-old fraud conviction

The ABC can reveal this is not Mr Joseph's first brush with the law in Texas.

In October last year, he was charged with indecency with a child by exposure, and spent a night in a Texas jail cell with a $US25,000 ($35,400) bond.

"I have not been indicted on either charge," Mr Joseph told the ABC.

"Anyone can be arrested on anything, doesn't mean they're guilty."

He said the charges were the result of an "ugly" break-up with a former romantic partner, and that "people get charged every day".

Brett Joseph told the ABC he was innocent and denied ever being convicted of fraud. (Supplied: Daisy Armstrong)

Brett Joseph has used multiple aliases. (Supplied: Daisy Armstrong)

Mr Joseph also denied he was a convicted fraudster here in Australia.

He was charged with eight offences relating to theft at the Griffith Local Court nearly a decade ago, but these were dismissed.

Four charges of receiving or disposing of stolen property were dismissed in 2017, while four charges of disposing of property were dismissed the following year.

But Mudgee Local Court records show Mr Joseph has been tried and convicted on three occasions for fraud-related crimes.

In 2016, he pleaded guilty to three counts of dishonestly obtaining property by deception.

He was fined $1,500 and also sentenced to 12 months' imprisonment, though this was suspended and he was put on a good behaviour bond.

Brett Joseph and Daisy Armstrong at the races 10 years ago while they briefly dated. (Supplied: Daisy Armstrong)

Brett Joseph and Daisy Armstrong briefly dated in 2016. (Supplied: Daisy Armstrong)

Mr Joseph said the public scrutiny he has been receiving for the past decade is the result of his "crazy b****" ex-girlfriend Daisy Armstrong, who has been running a public awareness campaign against him.

Speaking to the ABC, Ms Armstrong, also 39, said she has indeed unashamedly continued to publish information on Mr Joseph's whereabouts in a bid to warn others.

"Nothing has changed," she said in relation to the new charge.

"It's been 10 years since I first started blowing the whistle on him, and if he had learnt from his mistakes and become a better person, then of course we wouldn't still be on this train.

"I wish I could say that he might have learned his lesson, turned over a new leaf.

"At least people have a fighting chance to know who they're dealing with, which I didn't have," she added.

Daisy Armstrong, now, says she has moved on with her life but is happy to keep her website on Brett Joseph updated in a bid to warn others. (Supplied: Daisy Armstrong)

Ms Armstrong, from Griffith in NSW, dated Mr Joseph for six months in 2016 after meeting him on Tinder, but soon grew suspicious of some of his claims.

He had been living for free on her family's property, and she discovered a new dating profile where he had been misrepresenting himself as a wealthy farmer to attract other women while they were still together.

After starting a public website about Mr Joseph, she learned he went by multiple aliases, she said, including Brett Goodman, Hunter Ballieu, Brett Jones, Brett Inglis, Brett James and Brett Jay.

Brett Joseph has previously been previously convicted of fraud. (Supplied: Daisy Armstrong)

Another woman the ABC spoke to, Alanna O'Donnell, from Wollondilly Shire in NSW, said precious jewellery went missing after she lived with and dated Mr Joseph for several weeks back in 2009.

She was able to recover her antique ring years later, when she found the website about Mr Joseph and was shocked to discover Ms Armstrong had been gifted her ring.

This led to the theft charges against Mr Joseph in Griffith Court in 2017, but they were ultimately dismissed.

"I feel very let down by the Australian court system, that's for sure," Ms O'Donnell said.

"I feel very frustrated that the alarms were raised so early in Australia, but it's taken America to come in and hopefully put him away and stop that behaviour," she said of the new charges.

"I think it's just disgraceful that he's still going."

Ms O'Donnell recalled her six-week romance with him as a "whirlwind".

"It's like he consumes you in his personality," she said.

"[He] takes you on this whirlwind adventure, and you just don't even know you're in this cyclone until you start getting glimpses of things that don't necessarily add up.

"It's very trance-like. It feels so surreal: 'Somebody [who] finally loves me for who I am.'"

Brett Joseph has misrepresented himself in regional NSW. (Supplied: Daisy Armstrong)

Brett Joseph at an event in NSW several years ago. (Supplied: Daisy Armstrong)

Fraud detectives warning

Michael Gerondis, a retired fraud squad detective inspector and family friend of the Armstrongs, said he had been keeping tabs on Mr Joseph for years.

"He was saying that he was an agronomist," Mr Gerondis recalled, describing when he first met the fraudster.

"He couldn't even spell agronomist, but he came up with all these stories."

Mr Gerondis said like many fraudsters, Mr Joseph got away with some of his lies because they had "an element of truth to them".

"He told people that he had a huge cattle ranch in Australia. It did exist, it was a huge property, it just wasn't his," the ex-cop said.

Mr Gerondis said he was not surprised to see Mr Joseph has landed in hot water in the US.

"He's going to continue to do it [conduct himself fraudulently]. He can't help himself … I was surprised that it took so long," he said.

World.title: Nick Reiner could face death penalty if convicted of murdering parents
World.content:
A Los Angeles County grand jury has indicted Nick Reiner on murder charges in the killings of his parents, director Rob Reiner and Michele Singer Reiner, and added the allegation that he was lying in wait before attacking them.

Jake Reiner describes 'living nightmare' after parents' deaths Jake Reiner, the older son of Rob and Michele Reiner, says learning his parents were killed — and the aftermath of that — has been “too devastating to comprehend”.

The grand jury, which had been meeting in secret, returned the indictment on July 20.

It was unsealed on August 12 when Nick Reiner, 32, entered a not guilty plea.

The director, actor and Hollywood luminary Rob Reiner and his wife, photographer and producer Michele Singer Reiner, were stabbed to death in their home in the upscale Brentwood section of Los Angeles on December 14 last year.

Nick Reiner was arrested hours later and charged two days later.

Major step towards trial

The grand jury indictment is a major step toward trial and allows prosecutors to skip California's preliminary hearing process, where evidence is publicly aired.

Rob Reiner, Michele Singer, Romy Reiner, Nick Reiner, Maria Gilfillan and Jake Reiner on the red carpet in September 2025. (Reuters: Aude Guerrucci)

"This was a profound betrayal by someone who was loved and trusted by the very people he is accused of killing," Los Angeles County District Attorney Nathan Hochman said in a statement.

"We hope that by having a grand jury return an indictment in this case it will bring us one step closer to a trial and achieving justice."

The unsealed indictment reveals few new details in a case that has been shrouded in secrecy.

But the lying in wait allegation along with other circumstances mean Nick Reiner is eligible for the death penalty.

Prosecutors say they have not decided whether to seek it.

The indictment did not say how or why Nick Reiner was lying in wait.

It also included an allegation that he used a knife in the killing.

Authorities previously said the couple was stabbed.

Nick Reiner pleads not guilty to murder Nick Reiner has pleaded not guilty to two counts of first-degree murder in the fatal stabbing of his parents in December last year.

Many of the most basic questions about the killing remain publicly unanswered.

Prosecutors have said nothing about possible motives and leaks in the case have been virtually nonexistent on both sides.

The Los Angeles County chief medical examiner said he would like to make their autopsy reports public, but a court order has prevented him from doing so.

The LA County Public Defender's Office, which is representing Nick Reiner, declined to comment on the indictment.

World.title: Alan Jones trial live updates: Mother, ex-girlfriend of complainant ‘J’ to give evidence after legal issue triggers adjournment
World.content:
Warning: Graphic content

Hello and welcome to our live coverage of day seven of Alan Jones’ lengthy criminal trial on charges of indecent assault and sexual touching. Court reporter Clare Sibthorpe and I will be bringing you the latest from the hearing today.

If day seven looks familiar, you’re right. Yesterday was to be the seventh day of the trial, but the Crown foreshadowed that it wanted to amend seven of the charges in the case. This triggered an adjournment for the parties to make legal arguments.

Alan Jones arrives at the Downing Centre Local Court on Wednesday. KATE GERAGHTY

After hearing those arguments, Judge Glenn Walsh said the Crown did not require the court’s permission to make the changes, which do not relate to the alleged physical acts in the case. He concluded that it did not result in prejudice to Jones and his right to a fair trial.

The trial is expected to resume in earnest today in the NSW Local Court in Sydney’s historic Downing Centre building with more evidence relating to complainant “J”, the first witness to give evidence in the trial.

In the first week of the trial, the court heard allegations that Jones indecently assaulted “J”, a young athlete, starting with unwanted kissing when the man was a teenager in year 12. Jones denies the claims.

On Tuesday, the older brother of “J” and the complainant’s ex-girlfriend gave evidence about what they say he told them about the alleged assaults.

His brother said he had not witnessed Jones acting inappropriately towards “J”, but that the complainant told him in 2024, after Jones’ arrest, that he was one the men who had come forward.

The ex-girlfriend of “J” said he confided in her 20 years ago that Jones had touched him inappropriately. She said he looked like he had “seen a ghost” before he made the disclosure and swore her to secrecy.

Her evidence continues today. The mother of “J” and his former sporting coach are also slated to give evidence.

While we don’t expect to hear from him today, a man known as “C” will be the next complainant to give evidence. He may start his evidence as early as Friday.

The Crown alleges that Jones indecently assaulted or sexually touched six men without their consent between 2003 and 2020, and is seeking to prove 22 charges against him.

The former broadcaster has emphatically denied wrongdoing and his barrister Gabrielle Bashir, SC, said during her opening address to the court that the credibility and reliability of the complainants’ evidence would be tested.

Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) or the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491.

World.title: Telstra boss lands 11pc pay rise in year of 1200 job cuts
World.content:
Breaking TechnologyTelecommunications Telstra boss lands 11pc pay rise in year of 1200 job cuts David Swan August 13, 2026 — 8:49am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Telstra handed chief executive Vicki Brady an 11 per cent pay rise to $6.8 million last year, a bumper payday delivered against a backdrop of 1200 job cuts, and just weeks before a catastrophic network outage cut off Triple Zero calls. The telco’s direct workforce is now 4 per cent smaller, at 29,334, and Telstra has signalled it will keep cutting as it simplifies the business. The job losses lifted its redundancy bill by $92 million to $206 million. Telstra chief executive Vicki Brady apologised for last month’s outage. Louise Kennerley That cost-cutting helped drive a full-year result that has delivered shareholders a bigger dividend and a fresh $1 billion share buyback. Telstra’s full-year results to June 30 showed net profit rose 2.7 per cent to $2.4 billion, and core earnings climbed 3 per cent to $8.2 billion, even as group revenue dipped 0.8 per cent to $22.9 billion.



Related Article Telecommunications Your phone could switch networks when it loses coverage. Telstra says no Revenue at Telstra’s consumer arm, its largest, rose 0.7 per cent, and its infrastructure arm, InfraCo, rose 3.4 per cent. Those gains offset a 5.2 per cent fall in the enterprise business and an 11.3 per cent slump in the international unit. The mobile division remained a powerhouse. It added 274,000 users, though most of these were wholesale customers on rival brands using Telstra’s network, while its own retail postpaid handheld services actually went backwards. The average monthly postpaid bill rose 3.8 per cent to $56.20. The board lifted the full-year dividend by 10.5 per cent to 21 cents a share, 90.5 per cent of which is franked. The planned $1 billion buyback follows the $1.25 billion program completed in June. Brady said the buybacks sat “alongside increased capex and strategic investment” and allowed Telstra to lower its cost of capital. Addressing the July network outage, Brady said the company takes full responsibility and has hired an external expert to investigate.



“We know we let our customers down in July,” she said. “We have taken full accountability for this.” Brady said Telstra had an initial understanding of the root cause and had taken steps to address it, and would be “transparent about those findings and the actions we take as a result”. Telstra shed more than 1200 roles in the year leading up to the nationwide outage that left Australians unable to reach emergency services. Bloomberg She also acknowledged the outage had changed the conversation about the network. “Network resilience was brought into sharp focus,” she said, adding that Australians’ reliance on connectivity “will only grow”. The board did dock her for it. Directors cut Brady’s individual performance multiplier by 20 percentage points, stripping $607,000 from her bonus and leaving her with a short-term incentive of $2.762 million. Her total pay still rose 11 per cent.



Then-group executive of global networks and technology Shailin Sehgal took the same 20-point reduction. Every other senior executive lost 10 points, taking a further $1.29 million out of the leadership team’s bonus pool. Because the external investigation was still running when remuneration was signed off, the board has reserved the right to claw back more from FY27 pay once the findings land. Telstra has ruled out automatic payouts for the July blackout. It recently told a Senate hearing that just over 8000 claims resulted in slightly more than $100,000 being handed out, all in the form of bill credits. Related Article Updated

Telecommunications Full scale of Telstra network outage exposed Looking ahead, Telstra expects underlying earnings to grow to between $8.5 billion and $8.8 billion next year. To support that, it plans to spend up to $3.65 billion on capital works, with what it called a lift in network investment to apply lessons from the outage. However, the cost of major infrastructure projects, including its Aura fibre network, has blown out by $200 million to roughly $1.8 billion, driven by inflation and difficult site conditions. World.title: ASX set to slide; ANZ posts $1.9b quarterly profit, home loan applications fall
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to slide; ANZ posts $1.9b quarterly profit, home loan applications fall Stan Choe Updated August 13, 2026 — 8:11am ,first published 5:15am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Wall Street edged near its record after several AI stocks reported better growth than analysts expected, while a report showed inflation across the United States was slightly less bad last month. The S&P 500 added 0.3 per cent and marked its first gain since setting its all-time high on Friday. The Dow Jones Industrial Average slipped less than 0.1 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite climbed 0.5 per cent. Stocks like Nvidia and Super Micro Computer helped lead the way on signals that businesses continue to spend big dollars on AI infrastructure. Treasury yields eased following the latest inflation data. Wall Street jumped as the AI trade reignited after some positive results while a report showed inflation across the United States dipped. Bloomberg The Australian sharemarket is set to fall, with futures at 5.54am AEST pointing to a fall of 19 points or 0.2 per cent, at the open. The ASX lost 0.5 per cent on Wednesday. The Australian dollar was trading at US70.62¢. ANZ Bank says home loan applications have fallen 12 per cent since the May budget, excluding applications it received via a government deposit guarantee scheme, as it also reported $1.9 billion in cash profits for the latest quarter.



In a trading update for the June quarter, ANZ said its cash profits rose 1 per cent compared with the quarterly average for the March half. On Wall Street, stocks in the artificial-intelligence technology business helped lead the way after strong profit reports bolstered hopes they can continue to deliver big-enough growth to justify the huge gains their prices have made. Super Micro Computer, which sells servers and other equipment, jumped 19.6 per cent after reporting earnings per share for the latest quarter that were 84 per cent higher than analysts expected. It also gave forecasts for upcoming profit and revenue that topped analysts’ expectations. Related Article Opinion

Gold Gold is glittering again – but that’s not necessarily good news Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist CoreWeave, which offers AI computing power to customers over the cloud, leaped 19 per cent after reporting better revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected, along with a milder loss. CEO Michael Intrator said demand is accelerating from customers as big businesses adopt AI.



CoreWeave gives its customers access to AI chips from Nvidia, and Nvidia climbed 3 per cent. It was the single strongest force lifting the S&P 500. It’s a return to strength for AI stocks, which have been veering on a roller-coaster ride. After surging to records, AI stocks came under pressure on worries that they shot too high. Investors wanted to see big spenders on AI prove that their investments are yielding enough in profits and productivity to make them worth it. That in turn could lead to continued demand for chips and other AI infrastructure. Wall Street also got some support from easing yields in the bond market. Treasury yields fell after a report showed that US consumers paid prices for gasoline, groceries and other costs of living last month that were 3.4 per cent higher than a year earlier. That’s higher than anyone would like, but it’s not as bad as June’s 3.5 per cent inflation rate. The deceleration could give the Federal Reserve more leeway to hold off on hikes to interest rates. Higher rates would help keep a lid on inflation, but it would do so by making it more expensive for US households and companies to borrow and forcing a slowdown in the economy. Higher interest rates also would undercut prices for stocks and other investments.



The Fed’s members have been notably split about whether they should have already begun hiking interest rates. But Wednesday’s update on inflation pushed traders to pull back on bets the Fed will hike its main interest rate at its next meeting in September. Traders are betting on just a 40 per cent chance of it, down from the coin flip’s chance seen the day before, according to data from CME Group. That helped pull the yield on the 10-year Treasury down to 4.68 per cent from 4.70 per cent late Tuesday. It, though, still remains well above its 3.97 per cent level from before the war with Iran, which sent oil prices and worries about inflation spiking. Related Article Opinion

Property market Is it time to buy a house? Here is what the CBA chief would tell his kids Elizabeth Knight Business columnist Oil prices swung between modest gains and losses Wednesday, and the price for a barrel of Brent crude slipped 0.2 per cent to $US88.74.



Higher yields have already pulled long-term mortgage rates to their highest levels in a year. That’s hurting the housing industry, and losses for homebuilders on Wednesday helped keep the market in check. D.R. Horton fell 3.3 per cent, and PulteGroup lost 2.5 per cent. Builders FirstSource, which sells countertops and other building materials, dropped 1.9 per cent. In stock markets abroad, indexes were mixed across Europe and Asia. South Korea’s Kospi jumped 3.7 per cent for one of the world’s bigger gains. It’s been at the center of the jarring swings for AI stocks because it’s dominated by two tech giants, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix. AP The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.

The former broadcaster has emphatically denied wrongdoing and his barrister Gabrielle Bashir, SC, said during her opening address to the court that the credibility and reliability of the complainants’ evidence would be tested.

Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) or the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491.

World.title: Telstra boss lands 11pc pay rise in year of 1200 job cuts
World.content:
Breaking TechnologyTelecommunications Telstra boss lands 11pc pay rise in year of 1200 job cuts David Swan August 13, 2026 — 8:49am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Telstra handed chief executive Vicki Brady an 11 per cent pay rise to $6.8 million last year, a bumper payday delivered against a backdrop of 1200 job cuts, and just weeks before a catastrophic network outage cut off Triple Zero calls. The telco’s direct workforce is now 4 per cent smaller, at 29,334, and Telstra has signalled it will keep cutting as it simplifies the business. The job losses lifted its redundancy bill by $92 million to $206 million. Telstra chief executive Vicki Brady apologised for last month’s outage. Louise Kennerley That cost-cutting helped drive a full-year result that has delivered shareholders a bigger dividend and a fresh $1 billion share buyback. Telstra’s full-year results to June 30 showed net profit rose 2.7 per cent to $2.4 billion, and core earnings climbed 3 per cent to $8.2 billion, even as group revenue dipped 0.8 per cent to $22.9 billion.



Related Article Telecommunications Your phone could switch networks when it loses coverage. Telstra says no Revenue at Telstra’s consumer arm, its largest, rose 0.7 per cent, and its infrastructure arm, InfraCo, rose 3.4 per cent. Those gains offset a 5.2 per cent fall in the enterprise business and an 11.3 per cent slump in the international unit. The mobile division remained a powerhouse. It added 274,000 users, though most of these were wholesale customers on rival brands using Telstra’s network, while its own retail postpaid handheld services actually went backwards. The average monthly postpaid bill rose 3.8 per cent to $56.20. The board lifted the full-year dividend by 10.5 per cent to 21 cents a share, 90.5 per cent of which is franked. The planned $1 billion buyback follows the $1.25 billion program completed in June. Brady said the buybacks sat “alongside increased capex and strategic investment” and allowed Telstra to lower its cost of capital. Addressing the July network outage, Brady said the company takes full responsibility and has hired an external expert to investigate.



“We know we let our customers down in July,” she said. “We have taken full accountability for this.” Brady said Telstra had an initial understanding of the root cause and had taken steps to address it, and would be “transparent about those findings and the actions we take as a result”. Telstra shed more than 1200 roles in the year leading up to the nationwide outage that left Australians unable to reach emergency services. Bloomberg She also acknowledged the outage had changed the conversation about the network. “Network resilience was brought into sharp focus,” she said, adding that Australians’ reliance on connectivity “will only grow”. The board did dock her for it. Directors cut Brady’s individual performance multiplier by 20 percentage points, stripping $607,000 from her bonus and leaving her with a short-term incentive of $2.762 million. Her total pay still rose 11 per cent.



Then-group executive of global networks and technology Shailin Sehgal took the same 20-point reduction. Every other senior executive lost 10 points, taking a further $1.29 million out of the leadership team’s bonus pool. Because the external investigation was still running when remuneration was signed off, the board has reserved the right to claw back more from FY27 pay once the findings land. Telstra has ruled out automatic payouts for the July blackout. It recently told a Senate hearing that just over 8000 claims resulted in slightly more than $100,000 being handed out, all in the form of bill credits. Related Article Updated

Telecommunications Full scale of Telstra network outage exposed Looking ahead, Telstra expects underlying earnings to grow to between $8.5 billion and $8.8 billion next year. To support that, it plans to spend up to $3.65 billion on capital works, with what it called a lift in network investment to apply lessons from the outage. However, the cost of major infrastructure projects, including its Aura fibre network, has blown out by $200 million to roughly $1.8 billion, driven by inflation and difficult site conditions. World.title: ASX set to slide; ANZ posts $1.9b quarterly profit, home loan applications fall
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to slide; ANZ posts $1.9b quarterly profit, home loan applications fall Stan Choe Updated August 13, 2026 — 8:11am ,first published 5:15am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Wall Street edged near its record after several AI stocks reported better growth than analysts expected, while a report showed inflation across the United States was slightly less bad last month. The S&P 500 added 0.3 per cent and marked its first gain since setting its all-time high on Friday. The Dow Jones Industrial Average slipped less than 0.1 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite climbed 0.5 per cent. Stocks like Nvidia and Super Micro Computer helped lead the way on signals that businesses continue to spend big dollars on AI infrastructure. Treasury yields eased following the latest inflation data. Wall Street jumped as the AI trade reignited after some positive results while a report showed inflation across the United States dipped. Bloomberg The Australian sharemarket is set to fall, with futures at 5.54am AEST pointing to a fall of 19 points or 0.2 per cent, at the open. The ASX lost 0.5 per cent on Wednesday. The Australian dollar was trading at US70.62¢. ANZ Bank says home loan applications have fallen 12 per cent since the May budget, excluding applications it received via a government deposit guarantee scheme, as it also reported $1.9 billion in cash profits for the latest quarter.



In a trading update for the June quarter, ANZ said its cash profits rose 1 per cent compared with the quarterly average for the March half. On Wall Street, stocks in the artificial-intelligence technology business helped lead the way after strong profit reports bolstered hopes they can continue to deliver big-enough growth to justify the huge gains their prices have made. Super Micro Computer, which sells servers and other equipment, jumped 19.6 per cent after reporting earnings per share for the latest quarter that were 84 per cent higher than analysts expected. It also gave forecasts for upcoming profit and revenue that topped analysts’ expectations. Related Article Opinion

Gold Gold is glittering again – but that’s not necessarily good news Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist CoreWeave, which offers AI computing power to customers over the cloud, leaped 19 per cent after reporting better revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected, along with a milder loss. CEO Michael Intrator said demand is accelerating from customers as big businesses adopt AI.



CoreWeave gives its customers access to AI chips from Nvidia, and Nvidia climbed 3 per cent. It was the single strongest force lifting the S&P 500. It’s a return to strength for AI stocks, which have been veering on a roller-coaster ride. After surging to records, AI stocks came under pressure on worries that they shot too high. Investors wanted to see big spenders on AI prove that their investments are yielding enough in profits and productivity to make them worth it. That in turn could lead to continued demand for chips and other AI infrastructure. Wall Street also got some support from easing yields in the bond market. Treasury yields fell after a report showed that US consumers paid prices for gasoline, groceries and other costs of living last month that were 3.4 per cent higher than a year earlier. That’s higher than anyone would like, but it’s not as bad as June’s 3.5 per cent inflation rate. The deceleration could give the Federal Reserve more leeway to hold off on hikes to interest rates. Higher rates would help keep a lid on inflation, but it would do so by making it more expensive for US households and companies to borrow and forcing a slowdown in the economy. Higher interest rates also would undercut prices for stocks and other investments.



The Fed’s members have been notably split about whether they should have already begun hiking interest rates. But Wednesday’s update on inflation pushed traders to pull back on bets the Fed will hike its main interest rate at its next meeting in September. Traders are betting on just a 40 per cent chance of it, down from the coin flip’s chance seen the day before, according to data from CME Group. That helped pull the yield on the 10-year Treasury down to 4.68 per cent from 4.70 per cent late Tuesday. It, though, still remains well above its 3.97 per cent level from before the war with Iran, which sent oil prices and worries about inflation spiking. Related Article Opinion

Property market Is it time to buy a house? Here is what the CBA chief would tell his kids Elizabeth Knight Business columnist Oil prices swung between modest gains and losses Wednesday, and the price for a barrel of Brent crude slipped 0.2 per cent to $US88.74.



Higher yields have already pulled long-term mortgage rates to their highest levels in a year. That’s hurting the housing industry, and losses for homebuilders on Wednesday helped keep the market in check. D.R. Horton fell 3.3 per cent, and PulteGroup lost 2.5 per cent. Builders FirstSource, which sells countertops and other building materials, dropped 1.9 per cent. In stock markets abroad, indexes were mixed across Europe and Asia. South Korea’s Kospi jumped 3.7 per cent for one of the world’s bigger gains. It’s been at the center of the jarring swings for AI stocks because it’s dominated by two tech giants, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix. AP The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.

World.title: Cost-of-living crisis hits casino operator SkyCity, hundreds of jobs at risk
World.content:
Casino operator SkyCity is proposing a restructure which could affect 200 roles, citing economic challenges.

In a statement, the company said the restructuring would mainly be in its Auckland precinct.

Consultation started on Tuesday, and the company said it would continue over the next two weeks.

SkyCity said it was reviewing its operating model amid "sustained pressure on customers' discretionary spending", driven in part by the fuel crisis and cost-of-living challenges on both sides of the Tasman.

"The economic conditions facing our business are real, and they require us to make some hard choices about how we're set up for the future," SkyCity chief executive Jason Walbridge said.

"We're reshaping how our people are deployed across the group, so we're simpler, smarter and more connected."

Jason Walbridge. RNZ / Cole Eastham-Farrelly

SkyCity said it would change how staff were deployed across the business and become a "simpler, smarter and more connected" company.

It said any changes would be subject to "genuine consultation" with affected staff and their representatives.

"No decisions have been made," Walbridge said.

"We'll consult with our people before anything is finalised, and our focus remains on supporting them through any change and on building a stronger SkyCity."

SkyCity was due to report its full-year results next week and declined to be interviewed.

World.title: Pauline Hanna inquest adjourned while Polkinghorne documentary footage is narrowed down
World.content:
The inquest into the death of Pauline Hanna has been adjourned until Thursday afternoon, so footage from the cutting room of a documentary about her husband Philip Polkinghorne's criminal trial can be narrowed down.

Ms Hanna died in her Remuera home, which she shared with Polkinghorne in April 2021.

Dr Polkinghorne was found not guilty of murdering her in 2024.

At the Coroner's Court in Auckland on Wednesday, Coroner Tania Tetitaha ordered a documentary company, Blonde Razor Productions, to hand over four hours of raw footage from their interview with Dr Polkinghorne, which RNZ understands was filmed in 2022.

Excerpts of the interview were used in the documentary Polk: The Trial of Philip Polkinghorne, which aired on ThreeNow in 2025.

On Thursday morning, Coroner Tetitaha agreed to give Police counsel and interested parties in the inquest, including Dr Polkinghorne, who is being represented by his lawyer, Ron Mansfield, time to select clips of the interview to play in court after 2:15pm.

World.title: Church that owns historic Carlile House talks with Auckland Council about demolishing it
World.content:
Contemplating the future of Grey Lynn's abandoned Carlile House Morning Report Download MP3 3m

* This article has been updated to clarify Auckland Council was approached by the church regarding demolition, but this was prohibited.

Leaders of a church that owns a historic abandoned building in central Auckland have been in talks with Auckland Council about the possibility of demolishing it.

The once-grand, two storey Carlile House in Auckland's Grey Lynn was built in 1886 and has had many uses over its long life - including as an Anglican children's home, and an alternative school.

But in recent decades it has fallen into ruin and the church that owns it do not have the money to restore it to its former glory.

RNZ looks at the history and future of the building as part of our Abandoned Auckland series.

Architect and Grey Lynn local Graeme Burgess looks over a barbed wire and corrugated iron fence at the historic Carlile House on Richmond road in Grey Lynn.

"Right now, because of the fence running through here it actually feels so guarded, and it's like something that nobody can actually appreciate."

The building was grand in size and stature, but Burgess said after years of neglect it was heart-breaking to see the state it had ended up in.

"[It's] difficult to watch something so grand and so wonderful slowly falling apart. But there are reasons why it's in the state that it's in at present. And those reasons are incredibly complex."

The United Church of Tonga, which owned the building, did not have the money to do it up.

The church did not want to be interviewed for this story, but said it was working through its options for the building, and would put forward a plan in coming months.

Auckland Council said it had been approached about the possibility of demolishing the building by the church, but as it was a Category 1 Historic Place, that was prohibited.

The building was a Category 1 Historic Place RNZ / Marika Khabazi

Graeme Burgess hoped the church and council could find a way to make use of the place.

"I would hope that's not the discussions they're having. I hope that the discussions they're having would be about how the place can be retained to the greatest extent possible."

Local artist John Reynolds, who has lived opposite Carlile house for decades, was less optimistic - given the roof of the building had partially caved in.

"At the current rate of decay, in 18 months it'll be collapsing in on itself, if not before."

Reynolds believed the church had no interest in restoring the building, and the council had not done enough to help find a resolution.

In 2019, Auckland Council offered to buy the building, but the church declined.

At the time it was estimated re-developing it would cost $10 million to $20 million.

Reynolds would like the large property to be turned into social housing.

"It could be many houses, and it could be housing for people that needs housing. It could be a win for the community, a win for the church, and actually a win for the heritage nuts."

Local historian Tania Mace said Carlile house was originally built with money bequeathed by early Auckland businessman Edward Costley.

"He lived a very frugal life, he never owned his own home. In the end when he passed away he made a number of bequests and this was one of them. And the people of Auckland were shocked to find he was extremely, extremely, wealthy."

It was originally a training facility for disadvantaged young boys to learn technical skills.

Later it was an Anglican children's home, the headquarters of an evangelical outreach mission, an alternative school, and briefly a remand home, before eventually being bought by the United Church of Tonga in the late 1970s.

World.title: Māori and Pacific people have lower stigma towards mental illness - study
World.content:
Māori and Pacific people have a lower stigma towards people with mental illness than Europeans and Asians, according to a University of Otago study.

It found integrating Māori and Pacific attitudes towards mental illness into health campaigns may result in a less judgemental New Zealand.

Using data from the long running New Zealand Attitudes and Values Study (NZAVS), the study examined more than 58,000 participants' 'ratings of warmth' towards those with mental illness.

Lead author Issac Jamieson told RNZ the study analysed the relationship between ethnicity and mental health stigma in Aotearoa.

"Stigma has many different components to it, and we focused just on one stigmatising attitude, which was how participants rated their feelings of warmth towards those with mental illness. Now, the findings challenged previous narratives held by past research and the general public to some extent that certain ethnicities or indigenous populations are synonymous with greater mental health stigma."

Jamieson said a holistic or a collective worldview that Māori and Pacific people hold might be the reason for the lower stigma findings in the study.

He also pointed to Māori health models such as Te Whare Tapa Whā, in which mental wellbeing is one of four pillars of overall health and wellbeing.

Other Māori health and wellbeing models recognise that individuals are live in wider environment systems that impact them, he said.

"One of the other things we discuss as well is how Māori have developed a language around mental health that may actually be less stigmatising than what we traditionally use today. So we talk about the example of ADHD, which stands for Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder, and Māori have developed the word, aroreretini, which means the mind goes to many things.

"Culture is really central to us understanding and reducing mental health stigma. And I guess to better understand the stigma associated with mental health challenges, we must better understand how different cultures define and perceive these challenges.

"For every culture has these strengths or maybe different ways of viewing mental health challenges, which may actually help us to have less stigmatising language or methods."

It was important that mental health campaigns and research not only acknowledged, but also integrated different cultural perspectives when it came to tackling mental health stigma, he said.

"So what we really want is some culturally responsive interventions that take into account these different world views."

Jamieson said despite positive shifts over the past couple of decades, the stigma of mental illness continues to be prominent in society.

"The research is still saying that there's still work to be done. And the more research we have around trying to understand what might be associated with more or less stigma or how different cultures perceive these challenges, we're gonna be better placed to try and actually reduce it, reduce the stigma of mental health and improve the livelihood of those struggling at the moment."

The study was published in Kotuitui: New Zealand Journal of Social Sciences Online, authored by Issac Jamieson, Taylor Winter, Ririwai Fox, Aaron Hapuku, Edmond Fehoko, Andre Mason, Chris Sibley and Damian Scarf.
